#8593. Six Dumb Misconceptions About The Economy (that the Politicians Want You To Believe)

Well, it looks like we’re here in another US election year already.

As Advanced Mustachians, we already know that the ongoing battle of Harris vs. Trump should not be consuming much of our time.  Sure, we do our research and cast our votes but after that we move right on to focus on other things within our own circle of control.

But out of all the things the politicians like to bicker about, there’s one area where MMM does need to set the record straight, and that area is of course money. Your money, the economy in general, and the overall wealth of the nation.

Politicians are already not known for being the sharpest tools in the shed when it comes to technical stuff like science, technology, or economics. But this year the discourse has become particularly dumb, as our candidates try to manipulate undecided voters in swing states with ideas that are based on irrational emotions rather than sound economic sense.

For one particularly funny example, you may have noticed that the competing party (Trump in this case) is attacking the incumbents (Biden/Harris) over the “bad economy.” When in fact the US economy is stronger than it has ever been, with the lowest unemployment we’ve ever seen as well.

It’s hard to imagine a better situation than we have right now, and in fact the recent bout of higher inflation is a sign that things have been going too well, and we needed to step on the brakes with the help of higher interest rates.

But somehow the people still seem to believe that we have a “bad” economy. Take a look at this Gallup poll showing that while most people (85%) are doing really well right now, they assume that it’s just their own good fortune – only 17% believe the economy is doing well.

This is mathematically impossible, because if most people are doing well, that’s the definition of a good economy! And suspiciously enough, this widespread wrongness correlates quite nicely with the rise of social media misinformation.

So the politicians and the news have been doing the opposite of what they should be doing in an ideal situation (sharing accurate information). And sure, we can always just ignore their speeches and go on with our lives. But when it comes to economics, knowledge is power (and money). The more accurately we understand how things really work, the wealthier we will all become.

So with all that in mind, I hereby present you with my list of the…

Top Dumb Things Politicians Want You To Believe About The Economy

If there’s a recession, the opposition party likes to blame it on the current president. If the economy is booming, the current president likes to give himself (or possibly soon herself) credit for all of that success. But really, the US economy is way too big – and thankfully way too free – for the president to control or really even influence all that strongly.

In reality, our economy is a gigantic machine which converts labor and materials into things like iPhones, hospitals and pumpkin pies. And although we’re the biggest economy at 26% of the planet, we are still heavily influenced by that much bigger 74% of economic activity that the other 7.6 billion people on Earth are busy producing everywhere else.

When we have our inevitable little boom and bust cycles, they are mostly caused by the normal cycle of irrational exuberance (and greed) like the 2007 housing boom, followed by brief periods of extreme fear and pessimism like the 2008-2012 financial and housing crash.

The government does play a role too, by setting tax rates and other rules. But the effects of these policies are usually so delayed and unpredictable, that you can’t draw a straight line between today’s president and today’s economy. In other words, the government does its best to adjust the rudder on our giant ship, but in the short term our economy lurches around on the waves and storms of the ocean.

This one is especially funny to me, as our candidates feign sympathy for the hard life of middle class Americans, who now face higher borrowing costs on their credit cards and car loans and mortgages. They claim they will fight to bring the interest rates down. Trump even goes as far as bullying our Federal Reserve board members (who can only do their jobs if we allow them to function as independent experts) and suggesting that he would take over the whole department, if elected.

The real story is that while monetary policy would be a terrible tool to leave in the hands of a sitting president (see Argentina), it does function as an excellent set of gas and brake pedals for the economy if used properly. When things slow down and unemployment gets too high, a cut to the interest rates will produce a boost in everything from new jobs to stock prices. But if things get too hot, you get rapid inflation which can mess up the system.

3: Inflation has Made Life Harder for Americans (and the President Can Magically Reverse it)

This line of reasoning is even dumber than the last one. For a couple of years after the Covid era, we had rapid inflation. It was caused by a rare combination of a goods shortage caused by things like factory closures and remote work, plentiful demand from government stimulus spending and low interest rates. These factors have since ironed themselves out, and inflation is back down to an ultra-low 2.4%.

But most significantly, wages have still risen faster than inflation so we are all better off than before! Since 2019, overall prices are up 19% and our wages are up 21%. So even after all that inflation, we are still doing just fine. But the candidates are still bickering over inflation as if it’s an actual problem, and even worse promising to “bring prices back down”. And they’ve managed to convince the electorate that “higher wages and prices” is the same thing as “a bad economy”. Which is just plain wrong.

Bonus dumbness: politicians also occasionally blame “greedy corporations” for increasing prices to hoard profits. While price increases are totally acceptable in a market system (as a business owner you are free to set prices wherever you like), in reality it doesn’t usually happen because our markets are too competitive. For example, a recent deep analysis from NPR showed that no, grocery stores haven’t made any windfall profit at all off of this recent bout of Covid-fueled inflation.

One important thing that has changed over the past ten years is that US house prices and rents have both risen much faster than general inflation and even wages. On the positive side, interest rates have also risen which tends to make houses feel more expensive and is supposed to help bring house prices down. But it hasn’t happened yet which means we have the double whammy of higher prices and higher interest costs for mortgage borrowers.

The dumb part is that our candidates are proposing things that would make the problem even worse, like subsidies for first-time homebuyers or schemes to reduce the interest rates. When really the solution is to increase the supply of housing, which I personally think will happen if we stop putting up roadblocks for homebuilders (myself included) to build housing.

Things like faster and cheaper permits, less onerous and expensive building codes, eliminating suburban-style zoning and setback and car parking rules, and changing laws so that NIMBYs no longer get any say over what other people do with their own land could all help reduce the cost of building a house by about 50%, quickly and permanently.

5: The President Controls Gas Prices, and They Are Currently “High” and We Want Them Lower

Ahh, gasoline! The most ridiculous of things to worry about and the fuel for many of MMM’s rants since 2011.

First of all, on an inflation-adjusted basis, gasoline is still about the same price as it was in 1950: in the $3-4 range per gallon, in today’s dollars.

Secondly, it is so cheap that even with our huge inefficient American vehicles, the average household is still only spending 2.5% of their disposable income on the stuff! (The funny part is that they spend many times more on the rest of the car ownership experience while thinking gas is the part that is expensive)

Third, gasoline has been obsolete for almost a decade now. You can get a used electric car for less than the price of a comparable used gas car, or if you’re a fancypants money waster like me, new EVs are also cheaper than their gas counterparts. You get a faster, nicer car that almost never needs maintenance OR gasoline, and save money.

So why are we even still talking about this antique fuel of a previous era? Why aren’t the candidates also arguing over the price of Kodak film or typewriters or fax machines?

6: The Economy is Something We Should Even Worry About

The funniest part about all this economic talk is that we’re focusing on the wrong thing. While hard work and business and advancing the frontiers of human knowledge are all fun things, the reality is that we passed the point of having “Enough” decades ago. When the American middle class complains about how hard we have it these days, it’s like a bunch of overfed people at a buffet wishing they could just have one more flavor of donuts stacked onto the table.

Yes, we have income and wealth inequality so that the rich tend to get richer more quickly. And yes, we should keep that in check with a somewhat progressive tax system because a more equal society tends to be a more peaceful and happy one.

But have you noticed that as the rich people get richer, they don’t get any happier? It’s because after you pass the point of “Enough”, adding more money doesn’t really help much.

And “Enough” is much more defined by your mindset (and your collection of life skills) than your paycheck. So if the politicians really cared about improving our happiness and wellbeing, they’d be preaching the Principles of Mustachianism rather than pandering to the specific requests of coal miners or billionaires.

But alas, winning an election is a very different thing than proposing stuff that is actually best for the country. And for that reason, we cast our votes for the best party and then tune back out until the next election.

Autarky is the end goal of all these tariffs, and it has negative economic consequences that seem to be missing from what the politicans say. Without the ability to trade, countries lose the benefits of specialization and comparative advantage. This leads to higher prices for in country consumers and a lack of diversity in available goods. Autarky stifles innovation and technological progress by isolating a country from global competition and advancements. An autarkic system is also more vulnerable to domestic economic shocks, such as natural disasters or supply disruptions, because it cannot rely on imports to balance shortfalls. Autarky reduces a country’s economic growth potential by cutting off access to international markets, foreign investment, and trade-driven employment opportunities. Finally, it risks diplomatic isolation, as trade restrictions often result in retaliatory measures from other nations, further limiting a country’s global economic and political influence. While autarky may appeal in terms of self-reliance, the downsides—higher costs, reduced growth, and vulnerability—make it unsustainable in the modern country.

1. “Government deficits don’t necessarily cause inflation. They are funded by the sale of T-bills and bonds.”

Yes, but if demand for those bonds is weak, the central bank steps in as the lender of last resort, printing money to purchase them, which can lead to inflation.

2. “Even an expanding money supply does not dictate the inflation rate. As we saw last year, we can have inflation even when the money supply shrinks, and this year we have much lower inflation even with a growing money supply.”

Yes, but inflation often lags behind changes in the money supply—it can take time for new money to fully circulate and impact prices.

3. “Moderate inflation is NOT bad and does not destroy purchasing power (unless you keep your wealth all in cash).”

Inflation does destroy purchasing power. Investing in assets that grow faster than inflation, like stocks or real estate, can keep you ahead of it. They don’t avoid inflation, they just try to beat it.

Mr. Money Mustache October 30, 2024, 7:23 pm

I think hybrids were great as a transition technology, because they helped our gas cars become more efficient back when batteries were too expensive to make an affordable all-electric car.

For example, in 2013, electric car battery packs cost about $780 per kWh to build, meaning my Tesla Model Y’s 80 kWh pack alone would have cost $62,000!

Today (2024 as I write this) that battery pack number is about $100, so my battery is only $8k of the car’s price. And since an electric car no longer needs an engine, transmission, exhaust system or all the other junk that comes with combustion, we now see electric cars have become LESS expensive than gas cars of equivalent quality/performance (the model Y is in the low $40s brand new, and under $30k used)

With the combination of easy+cheap home charging plus a bunch of nationwide fast charging networks (Tesla’s is still the best by far), there is no reason to have to settle for a hybrid – unless you’re shopping in the cheaper end of the used market. An under $10k used Prius with low miles is still a great frugal car if you can find one!

Avoid Nissan Leafs since their charging standard is no longer used and their batteries are air cooled, leading to far more degradation than other EVs that have active cooling. If you’re looking at Chevy Bolt’s make sure the battery modules were repaired per the recall. One of the best things about them is that your house is your “fuel” station. If you don’t have at home charging available it can be more of a challenge (unless your work has chargers).

Our 2014 Leaf that we bought used for a song in 2019 is still doing exactly what we need it to do – around town car, usually under 10 miles per day (eBike would be even more economical, but I kinda like my climate control here in the very hot, very humid southeast). If you’re needing to do a lot of long-distance driving, then yeah – Leaf’s, particularly older ones aren’t a great choice.

Agreed on at-home charging still the best way – public charging is expanding, but paid public charging is often as expensive as gasoline.

https://www.autotempest.com/ aggregates a bunch of different used car sales websites & has filters to make searching really easy.

Social Security receives annual cost of living adjustments. Defined benefit pensions almost always adjust for inflation. Private retirement account can and should be very easily invested in interest bearing securities or the stock market. I’m a city dweller with a desk job, so take this analysis for what its worth. Also, a farm or ranch is a business, so a approaching it from a personal finance perspective may not be the right way to look at it.

From what I understand most small farms and ranches in the US aren’t profitable. Based on my parents’ neighbors and many of the sources I’ve read, I think this is because farming and ranching is often a cultural identity and a lifestyle choice, and these properties aren’t being run as an efficient business. They’re hobby farms run by rich dentists, or their owners identify as “cattle ranchers” whether or not the market supports that identity and without a diversified, efficient business plan to maximize the profitability of the entire enterprise.

Here are some Mustachian principles I think apply to farms, ranches, and people who live in rural areas.

Trade the pickup truck for a smaller, less expensive, and preferably used vehicle that does the job better and drive it as little as possible. For everything else, buy a bike or small (used) sedan. There are shades of rural, but a lot of transportation needs can still be met by bike or electric bike. I rode my ebike about 40 miles yesterday to run errands in the city. I grew up in the sticks, and I’d have had a lot more freedom if I’d had an ebike. An electric cargo bike may able to be substituted for a four-wheeler or pickup truck for a lot of on farm transportation. The bike I have can basically carry the weight of two people. If you’re moving a dozen 40lb bags of feed around, that’s a max of four trips by electric cargo bike. Bikes are low, so loading one is faster and easier than throwing bags up into a pickup truck bed.

When it comes to farm equipment and purchases of all kinds, ask if you really need the equipment or if its just a status symbol. Can the job be done with muscle power. If you need the equipment, can you buy it used or substitute a less flashy alternative. Financing for farm equipment is similar to financing for a new car. Probably a money hole.

Every single farm input needs scrutiny and optimization. Fertilizer that washes into the river is money going down the sewer. This includes water, fertilizer, pesticides, etc. Spraying money at the problem isn’t solving it.

Cut your Cash-Leaking Umbilical Cord. If you moved to the country to enjoy the country, why do you need 500 channels of entertainment?

Focus on your Circle of Control, not your Circle of Interest. You can’t change the global cattle market, but you can decide whether to add sheep and goats, get paid by a land conservancy, host duck hunters, market your beef to yuppies at farmers markets, or do any number of other things to increase the profitability of your property.

Reduce grocery trips and expenses by growing your own food and trading with neighbors. Put in some fruit trees and a kitchen garden. Raise some chickens. Trade for milk. This should be one of the big advantages of living in the countryside in farm country.

That’s just a quick look, but I think a lot of the Mustachian principles apply in rural areas too.

Most phone plans charge less for each line as more lines join one account, so relatives or friends paying for separate plans can each pay less by sharing one. Check the plan’s price at your exact number of lines, and share only with people you trust, since the account owner owes the whole bill.

AT&T’s Value 2.0 unlimited plan costs $50 a month for one line but $30 a line for four, with AutoPay from a bank account and paperless billing.

Two lines cost $45 each and three cost $35 each, all before taxes and fees. So four relatives each paying $50 for a line of their own on that plan spend $200 a month, while the same four on one account pay $120. Together they save $960 a year.

Many prepaid brands, which run on a major carrier’s network for less, cut the price per line too. Total Wireless’s MAX 5G plan, on Verizon’s network, costs $50 for one line, $40 a line for two, about $32 for three, and about $26 for four. Those prices already take off its AutoPay discount and include taxes and fees. Not every plan works this way. Verizon’s Simplicity plan charges a flat $45 a line with Auto Pay and paper-free billing, however many lines you add.

Share with relatives or friends whose payments you’d count on. At AT&T, the account owner is responsible for the whole bill, so an unpaid share can bring a late fee and put every line on the account at risk of suspension. AT&T’s SplitPay can text each person the share for their line, with a link to pay it.

Plan for someone leaving, too. On AT&T, the account owner starts a transfer of billing responsibility, and the person leaving accepts it. That moves the line and its number to that person’s own account. They must pass AT&T’s credit check, and any phone still being paid off on the line must be paid off or transferred first. The lines that stay then pay the higher per-line price of a smaller account.

Price the plan at the exact number of lines you’d have before anyone joins, and write down each person’s share and the day it’s due.

To pick the plan your group will share, compare the best cheap cell phone plans.

Can you count on Social Security in retirement? While the retirement trust fund is projected to run out in 2032, according to the 2026 Trustees Report, benefits will still be paid out, just at a lower percentage. How much lower? 78% of scheduled benefits. That’s a 22% reduction, which is real. But it’s not a 100% reduction!

On average, heirs typically receive inherited IRAs at age 59, and the mean balance of those accounts is $128,000, according to a recent Vanguard report. Those accounts can be a sizable windfall, but taxes could take a chunk without proper planning, experts say. Original account owners may consider Roth conversions, strategic beneficiaries moves and other tactics.

When it comes to investing, people fixate on the risks of the stock market: What if the market crashes? Will I get the return I expected? How much can I draw down from investments each year without running out of money? Those are all valid concerns. But they are far from the only risks out there. What’s more, if you spend too much time focusing on just one risk then you are liable to make poor decisions.

The SpaceX and Anthropic IPOs are every money lesson in miniature: There’s the gap between the number on the screen and the money you can actually spend, the tax bill that stalks you home from the party, the way a big, sudden pile of money makes smart people stop thinking clearly. You don’t need stock options to learn any of that. You just need to see it laid out simply enough that the shame falls away.

Finding bliss is centered around not looking for it. Pursuing feelings is a road to nowhere. Fixating on yourself is a recipe for an unsatisfactory life. It turns out being altruistic or pursuing something greater than your self engages the brain’s reward systems.

#8590. IRS Audit Red Flags – Back Each One With Records Instead of Skipping Deductions

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Few returns get an IRS audit, but some features raise the odds, such as 1099 income missing from the return, deductions large for your income, and business costs that look personal or estimated. Keep receipts, logs, and statements behind those lines as you go, and claim every deduction you can back up.

The IRS audited about 3 of every 1,000 individual returns filed for 2021, the latest year with near-final figures in its Data Book. Filers with $25,000 to $500,000 of income before losses faced about 2 in 1,000, those with $1 million to $5 million about 1 in 100, and those with $10 million or more about 1 in 15.

What’s on the return matters too. The IRS gets a copy of every W-2 and 1099 filed under your name, plus the W-2G for gambling winnings, and matches them against your return, so income left off shows up. Its computers also compare each return with similar ones.

These lines draw a closer look, so check your return for them before you file:

None of these lines is a reason to skip a deduction you’re owed. Each is a reason to keep records behind it. A freelance photographer who deducts all her car and phone costs without logs has only a guess to offer when an auditor asks how much of that use was personal. With a mileage log kept as she drives and a business-use percentage for each, she can prove the business share she deducts.

The IRS’s usual window to audit a return is three years, so keep tax records at least that long, and some longer.

Log each expense and business drive when it happens, not at tax time, since IRS Publication 463 gives a record made at the time more weight than one written up later.

For a place to keep those records, compare the best online bookkeeping services.

More than 60% of respondents in a 2026 Goldman Sachs survey of 5,106 working and retired Americans said they had taken work outside their primary job, most out of necessity rather than a wish for extra spending money. Nearly 70% had delayed a major financial goal.

Retirement is increasingly becoming a touchy topic for many, especially those of us who are used to a certain level of stability.

The news only makes matters worse. On Friday, October 30, we saw Nasdaq’s biggest 1-day drop since June 5, setting the internet ablaze with speculation. The index closed 7.8% below its October 6 record, though it was noted that the S&P 500 was only a few percent below its own record.

Then there’s inflation. Annual inflation reached 3.7% in September, up from 3.4% in August. Pair that with continuing international conflicts on several fronts, and you’ve got the perfect storm of insecurity.

A National Institute on Retirement Security survey found that 80% of Americans say that the nation faces a retirement crisis and 61% worry they won’t be financially secure in retirement.

The respondents blamed inflation (73%) and market volatility (62%) as contributing factors, and 76% feared Social Security cuts if Congress fails to act.

A New York Life survey of more than 2,000 adults found that 34% had already delayed retirement or planned to, and 46% of them expected to push it back 5 years or more. Their top reasons were a lack of savings (46%) and inflation (45%).

Those who have already retired aren’t immune to these insecurities. The Goldman Sachs sample included 1,494 retirees aged 45 to 75. A market drop may also hurt more when you’re drawing from a portfolio than when you’re adding to it.

So, wondering if you should go back to work feels like a warranted question. Plenty of retirees take the leap back. Doctors go back too, though plenty of them say they don’t miss it. In a recent r/emergencymedicine thread, retired ED physicians were split on the question.

One, 3 years out, said he doesn’t miss it at all and still has the occasional nightmare. Another quit at 61 with no plan, misses the people and belonging to the group and keeps looking for work without luck.

1.5 million retirees reentered the workforce by March 2022.

We spend decades planning for the day we stop working. Then some of us stop, and a year or 2 later we’re checking job boards or answering calls from our old group. If that sounds like you, this article is for you.

Let’s take a look at the reasons many doctors feel the urge to un-retire, what going back to work in 2026 entails and the logistics of it all.

In case you missed it: Micro-retirements aren’t a shortcut to FIRE

Money is the top reason many retirees choose to go back, so let’s start there. A recent survey found that 48% of working retirees said they needed the income, while 45% said they worked for social and emotional benefits.

Divide 1 year of spending by your portfolio. An example in T. Rowe Price’s example illustrates a 62-year-old with $900,000 who spends $65,000 a year.

That’s a 7.2% withdrawal rate. She has a 64% chance of not outliving her money if she retires at 62, a 91% chance at 65 and a 97% chance at 67.

Now let’s imagine a physician-specific version.

Say you have $2,500,000 and spend $150,000 a year before taxes. That’s a 6% withdrawal rate. A part-time job paying $60,000 would trim your withdrawals to $90,000, which is 3.6%.

You lower your rate by 2.4 percentage points without changing how you live. Of course, taxes will reduce that paycheck so ask your planner for a clearer outline.

One retired doctor said he saved about 30% of his take-home pay in his last years of full-time work, and his spending ended up around half of his colleagues’.

He could walk away any day, and his group knew it. That kind of freedom is helpful even after you return because you’re able to negotiate better when you don’t actually need the job.

Before you take a job, figure out whether the problem is your portfolio or your spending. If your withdrawal rate looks fine but spending still makes you uneasy, a concrete spending plan may help more than a paycheck. Ask your planner to set a monthly amount you can spend without second-guessing.

Working longer also helps in 2 other ways. You can delay account withdrawals as well as Social Security. Benefits grow 8% for every year you wait past full retirement age until you reach 70, while claiming at 62 cuts them by almost 30%.

Continuing to work also gives you more time to contribute to your retirement accounts. If your new employer offers a 401(k) or 403(b), the 2026 limit is $24,500, plus an $8,000 catch-up at 50 and older or $11,250 at ages 60 to 63.

It depends on whether you’ve claimed it and how old you are. If you haven’t claimed, going back to work is straightforward and your eventual monthly SS check will continue to increase.

If you claimed before full retirement age (FRA), the earnings test applies. In 2026, Social Security withholds $1 for every $2 you earn above $24,480 if you’re under FRA all year.

In the year you reach FRA, the limit rises to $65,160, and the agency withholds $1 for every $3 above it. Only earnings before the month you reach FRA count.

If your part-time schedule pays more than $24,480, expect withholding. The money isn’t gone for good, though. Social Security recalculates your benefit at FRA to credit the months it withheld.

Only wages and self-employment earnings count, so investment income doesn’t trigger withholding. Once you reach FRA, working doesn’t reduce your benefit.

You’ll also keep paying Social Security taxes on your paychecks. Higher earnings can also make more of your benefit taxable, so ask your tax preparer to estimate that too.

What if you changed your mind after claiming early? If you claimed before FRA, you have 12 months to withdraw your application. You must repay what you received, and Social Security then treats your record as if you never claimed at all.

Coverage before 65 costs far more in 2026 than it did in 2025 since the enhanced ACA subsidies expired on December 31, 2025.

KFF reports that a 60-year-old with a $65,000 income now pays an average of $10,389 more per year, or $865 per month. The subsidy cliff is also back which means above 400% of the poverty level (which is $62,600 for a single person in 2026), you lose the premium tax credit entirely.

On top of that, the ACA allows insurers to charge adults in their 60s up to 3 times what they charge adults in their 20s.

So a job with group health coverage may save you thousands of dollars a year because it skips the marketplace and the income cliff.

A working physician said that if he left medicine early, he’d take a flexible management job of about 25 hours a week mostly for the group insurance and the 401(k) match.

If you’re considering the same, ask HR what hours are required for benefits and when coverage starts, since each plan sets its own cutoff.

Medicare changes much of the picture. If you delayed Part B because you had coverage through your own or your spouse’s current job, you get an 8-month special enrollment period after that job or coverage ends.

If you miss it, you’ll have to pay 10% more for each full 12-month period you could have had Part B, for as long as you keep it. COBRA and retiree coverage don’t count for that exemption.

Keep in mind that Medicare generally pays first if the employer has fewer than 20 employees. So a small practice’s plan may pay second and you’d still need Part B.

Learn more: 11 Retirement Planning Mistakes That Haunt High-Earning Physicians

Don’t count on getting your old job back.

An AARP survey of more than 3,500 people ages 50 and older found that 74% believe their age will be a barrier to getting hired, and 64% of workers 50 and older have seen or experienced age discrimination at work. That stigma is even worse for women.

Another AARP report found that 37% of workers 50 and older experienced subtle age discrimination during a job search in 2025, up from 30% in 2024. These surveys cover all fields, not only medicine, so ask recruiters in your specialty what they are seeing firsthand.

Think about what you want the next job to be. 24% of workers 50 and older planned a job change in 2025, so you won’t be the only one looking. If your retirement was driven mostly due to clinical work, teaching, consulting or chart review may suit you better than your old schedule.

We’ve already established that money drives about half of all unretirements. Boredom and a wish to help others drive many of the rest.

In an AARP survey, 18% of unretirees said boredom or a desire to stay active was their main reason for returning to work. For doctors, these sentiments start even before they leave.

In a Jackson Physician Search survey, 44% of physicians feared losing their sense of purpose in retirement and 39% feared boredom (money was still the top fear at 53%).

In CHG Healthcare’s 2024 survey, physicians who wanted to keep working felt that way because of a love of medicine (58%), social connections (57%) and concern for patients (39%). Others stated not feeling emotionally ready (47%), wanting to keep their lifestyle (35%) and fearing boredom or isolation (33%).

In Medscape’s 2025 retirement report, the top reason physicians gave for not retiring earlier was feeling they still had more to offer (62%), ahead of not having enough saved (45%). In the 2023 report, 46% expected retirement to feel like losing a part of their identity.

Retired and soon-to-retire ED physicians on Reddit offer a mixed bag of insights. One commenter who was 4 months from retiring expects to miss the ego boost of being a doctor. The one who quit at 61 with no plan misses colleagues and most of his patients, though not the fatigue of rotating shifts or the dread of sending home someone who should have stayed. Several said sleep and a normal daytime rhythm were the biggest change.

Retirement also changes what stresses you out. A 2025 Mayo Clinic review of physician well-being in retirement says that stress moves from work problems to personal ones, including professional identity, family, health and the loss of relationships.

The journal’s late-career paper urges physicians to plan for social and emotional needs along with finances. If you can’t picture your days without the work and the people, look at part-time options before you retire fully.

Give your first year in retirement a fair shake before you decide. People who leave long, consuming careers often describe a rocky start to retirement.

One user on Reddit said that it took about a year to stop feeling guilty about doing nothing. Another lasted 2 years, took a part-time job and has stayed 10 years. A third said the new job mattered to them mostly for the community, since all their friends still worked.

In case you missed it: The Nightmare Before Retirement: A Physician’s Cautionary Tale (2026 Edition)

If burnout pushed you out in the first place, the same job will push you out again. In 2026, burnout in healthcare is still running rampant.

Doximity’s May 2026 poll found that 82% of physicians say they’re overworked and 46% are considering early retirement because of it.

That number is up from 37% in 2025 and 21% in 2021. The jump is sharpest among women (54% in 2026 compared to 33% in 2023) and physicians ages 50 to 54 (56%, up from 35%).

Medscape’s 2026 burnout report corroborates this. 50% of male and 51% of female physicians say that their work causes their burnout, and 13%–14% are considering leaving medicine altogether.

In a MedCentral survey, 44% of physicians said they had considered leaving medical practice since the start of the year.

The 2026 tax rules changed how charitable gifts are deducted. Join Earned and Physician on FIRE to learn what changed, how to give more tax-efficiently, and what to do before year-end.

Featuring Carole Foos, CPA, Managing Director at Earned, and Jorge Sanchez, MD, of Physician on FIRE.

Takeaway: A practical year-end giving checklist to help you act before December 31.

Tue, Nov 17  ·  2:30 pm ET  ·  11:30 am PT

A recent AMA study in The Permanente Journal looked at doctors who had already left and found that 971 clinically inactive physicians were typically 48.1 years old when they left clinical practice. Their top reasons were the hassle factor (44.7%), stress (44.5%), unrealistic patient demands (41.1%) and lack of professional satisfaction (38.4%).

Most doctors don’t plan to go cold turkey, however. In CHG Healthcare’s late-career survey, 63% of respondents said they’d rather work less than not work at all and 94% had at least slight interest in locum tenens work.

26% of physicians from a Weatherby Healthcare survey say that they are interested in locum tenens work. That’s 7 points higher than last year and the highest in 10 years.

If the actual reason behind your retirement still rings true or any of the reasons stated above give you a pause, you may want to reconsider jumping back into the workforce. Unless financial insecurity is twisting your arm, there’s no point in going back to something that already burned you out.

Fortunately, there are many other work options for physicians that don’t involve selling your soul. Locum tenens and expert witness work are popular ways for physicians to keep working.

Learn more: Physician Side Gigs That Actually Pay in 2026

Rules vary by state so check what’s needed where you live. Florida requires a reactivation fee, proof of continuing medical education (CME) for each year the license was inactive or retired, a health history and a financial responsibility form.

Pennsylvania requires full Board review and possibly proof of competency. According to the AAMC some states require a reentry program after an absence that averages about 3 years.

The ED physician who quit at 61 let his board certification lapse and said he now wishes he’d kept it, because it might have opened insurance work.

Another retired ED doctor commented that he dreamed for 2 years about working shifts without a license or malpractice cover. The roles you want to work in may or may not require these credentials so check before you make up your mind.

Most carriers give retiring physicians tail coverage free or at low cost. But some carriers may cancel that tail or charge a premium if you resume practice because when you return to clinical practice and receive pay or compensation for clinical work, you violate the retirement condition under which the tail fee was waived. Check with your provider.

The AMA warns that some physicians’ retirement income may change if they take paid work. Check your pension plan before you accept a role.

Of course, there’s no universal right answer and no rulebook that says you must make one permanent decision.

Start by being honest about why you feel the urge to return. If it’s your portfolio that’s got you worried, earning an income may give you some much-needed breathing room.

If you miss the people, intellectual challenge or sense of purpose, you might find what you’re looking for in a very different role.

But if you’re simply uncomfortable with having more time than you’ve ever had before, give yourself a little longer before dusting off your resume.

Most importantly, don’t let a bad week in the market convince you that decades of retirement planning have failed. Nor should you feel obliged to return to medicine because you miss being a physician. It’s okay to miss parts of your career without wanting the whole thing back.

And no matter what you decide, don’t let your credentials lapse. Your medical license and board certification represent years of hard work and keeping them active preserves options you may not realize you’ll want later.

Even if you’re 100% certain you’ll never practice again, give your future self the benefit of the doubt. You don’t have to use those credentials, but you might one day wish you still had them.

Also read: The Idea of “Retiring to” Something

It depends on your finances, personal goals and reasons for retiring. Returning to work can provide income, health insurance and social connections, but it shouldn’t come at the expense of the retirement you worked so hard to achieve.

The most common reasons include financial insecurity, boredom, loss of purpose, social isolation and missing the intellectual challenge of their former careers.

Yes. Retired physicians can return to clinical practice, provided they meet their state medical board’s licensing and reactivation requirements. They may also need to address CME, board certification and malpractice coverage.

Yes, if you claim Social Security before full retirement age. In 2026, benefits are withheld if your earnings exceed $24,480, or $65,160 in the year you reach full retirement age. The earnings test no longer applies once you reach FRA.

Keeping your medical license active preserves the option to return to clinical practice without going through the full reactivation process. Check your state’s renewal requirements and consider maintaining board certification, too.

There’s no set waiting period. Give yourself time to adjust to retirement and understand what’s driving your desire to return. If finances aren’t forcing the decision, consider giving retirement at least a year before making a move.

This was a really thoughtful look at a question with no single right answer. The withdrawal-rate example was especially clear — seeing how part-time work could bring a 6% rate down to 3.6% makes the math feel much less abstract. I also had not realized how much the 2026 ACA subsidy changes could push someone back toward a job with group coverage. The advice to keep a license and board certification active, even when you are sure you are done, seems like wise insurance for your future self.

#8588. The Hotel’s Member Rate Often Beats the Booking App – Check It Before You Book

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Before you book a chain hotel through a booking app, check the chain’s own site, signed in to its free loyalty program. Members often pay no more there than on the app, and booking through the app forfeits the chain’s points and credit toward elite status. Compare the same room, dates, and cancellation terms at the final price.

A booking app doesn’t sell a big hotel chain’s member rate. The chain sells that discount to members of its free loyalty program on its own site and app.

Hilton takes at least 2% off eligible rates for members who book on its site or app, and Marriott’s member rate is at least 2% below the hotel’s lowest public rate for a standard room on weekdays.

Booking through an app also costs you the chain’s rewards. At Hilton, a reservation made through a third-party site earns no points and no credit toward elite status, the program’s higher tiers. It also gets none of the member perks, such as free Wi-Fi and late checkout when available. Changes and cancellations go through the site you booked with, not Hilton.

On the app and on the chain’s site, signed in, choose the same room type, dates, and cancellation terms. Then compare the totals on the last screen before payment, taxes and fees included. Say the app’s total comes to $189 a night for a room you can cancel up to a day ahead, and the chain’s site comes to $176 for the same room on the same terms. Booking direct at $176 rather than $189 saves $13 a night and earns points.

When the app still comes out cheaper than the chain’s site, the big chains offer a price match. Hilton’s Price Match Guarantee, for one, matches another site’s public price at least 1% below Hilton’s for the same room and terms when you book direct and claim within 24 hours. It then takes another 25% off the room rate. It doesn’t cover travel packages, opaque deals that name the hotel only after you book, or prices shown only after signing in or only in a mobile app.

The app can still win on a flight-and-hotel package, an opaque deal, or a last-minute discount, and at an independent hotel with no loyalty program. Equal totals favor the chain’s own site, since the same price there also earns points and elite credit, and the hotel itself handles any change.

Choose the app you compare against from the best hotel booking apps.

#8587. 13 Best Investment Opportunities for Accredited Investors

Home » Invest » 13 Best Investment Opportunities for Accredited Investors

Unlock the exclusive world of accredited investing where the stakes are high, the opportunities are vast, and the rewards can be game-changing. From hedge funds to venture capital delights, embark on an investment journey that only a select few have the privilege to explore.

When I became an accredited investor, I found myself among an elite group with the financial means and regulatory clearance to access investments that many couldn’t. This opened doors to exclusive realms like hedge funds, venture capital firms, specific investment funds, private equity funds, and more.

Even though I had this “exclusive access” it took me a while to start investing in alternative asset classes.

The Securities and Exchange Commission states that as an accredited investor, I possess a level of sophistication that equips me to craft a riskier investment portfolio than a non-accredited investor. While this might not be universally true for everyone, in my case, I had demonstrated the financial resilience to bear more risk (see barbell investing), especially if my investments took an unforeseen downturn.

One of the intriguing aspects I discovered was that investment opportunities for accredited investors aren’t mandated to register with financial authorities. This means they often come with fewer disclosures and might not be as transparent as the registered securities available to the general public.

The underlying belief is that my status as a sophisticated investor implies a deeper understanding of financial risks, a need for less disclosure of unregistered securities, and a conviction that these exclusive investment opportunities are apt for my funds.

On a personal note, as a practicing CFP®, I haven’t always worked with accredited investors. Early in my career, I didn’t quite grasp the allure. However, as time went on, I began to see the broader spectrum of investment options available to accredited investors.

As I learned more the clearer it became why this realm was so sought after. The variety and potential of these exclusive opportunities were truly eye-opening, reshaping my perspective on the world of investing.

An accredited investor is an individual or a business entity that is allowed to trade securities that may not be registered with financial authorities. They are entitled to this privileged access because they satisfy one or more requirements regarding income, net worth, asset size, governance status, or professional experience.

The concept of an accredited investor originated from the idea that individuals or entities with a higher financial acumen or more resources are better equipped to understand and bear the risks of certain investment opportunities.

Historically, the distinction between accredited and non-accredited investors was established to protect less experienced investors from potentially risky or less transparent investment opportunities.

Regulatory bodies, such as the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), have set criteria to determine who qualifies as an accredited investor, ensuring that they have the financial stability and sophistication to engage in more complex investment ventures.

To be classified as an accredited investor, one must meet specific criteria set by regulatory bodies:

Here’s a rundown of some of the top investments for accredited investors…

Fundrise has revolutionized the real estate investment landscape. By democratizing access to real estate portfolios, it allows individuals to invest without the complexities of property management or the need for vast capital. The platform’s innovative approach provides exposure to a traditionally lucrative, yet often inaccessible, sector of the market

Through Fundrise, investors can access a diversified range of properties, from commercial ventures to residential units. The platform’s expert team curates these portfolios, ensuring a balance of risk and reward. With its user-friendly interface and transparent reporting, Fundrise has become a top choice for many venturing into real estate investments.

Investors start by choosing a suitable investment plan on Fundrise. Once invested, the platform pools the funds with other investors and allocates them across various real estate projects. As these properties generate rental income or appreciation in value, investors receive returns in the form of dividends or appreciation.

Equitybee offers a unique platform that bridges the gap between private companies on the cusp of going public and potential investors. This innovative approach provides a golden opportunity for investors to tap into the potential of startups and other private firms before they make their public debut.

The platform’s primary focus is on employee stock options. By allowing investors to invest in these options, they can potentially benefit from their appreciation as the company grows. With a vast array of companies, from emerging startups to established giants, Equitybee presents a diverse range of investment opportunities.

Investors browse available stock options from various companies on Equitybee. Once they choose an option, they invest their funds, which are then used to purchase the stock options from the employees. If the company goes public or gets acquired, the investor stands to gain from the increased value of these stocks.

Percent stands as a beacon in the vast sea of the private credit market, illuminating a sector often overshadowed by traditional investments. This burgeoning market, valued at over $7 trillion, consists of companies borrowing from non-bank lenders. Percent offers a unique vantage point into this market, allowing investors to diversify their portfolios beyond typical stocks and bonds.

The allure of Percent lies in its ability to offer shorter terms and higher yields, combined with investments that are largely uncorrelated with public markets. This makes it an attractive proposition for those looking to step away from the volatility of traditional markets.

Upon joining Percent, investors are presented with a plethora of private credit opportunities. After selecting an investment, funds are pooled with other investors and lent out to companies seeking credit. As these companies repay their loans, investors earn interest, providing a steady income stream.

Masterworks paints a vivid picture of art investment, blending the worlds of finance and fine art. Traditionally, investing in art was a luxury reserved for the elite. However, Masterworks has democratized this, allowing individuals to buy shares in artworks from world-renowned artists.

The platform’s strength lies in its expertise. From authentication to storage, every facet of art investment is handled meticulously. This ensures that investors can appreciate both the beauty of their investments and the potential financial returns.

After registering on Masterworks, investors can browse a curated selection of artworks. They can then purchase shares, representing a fraction of the artwork’s value. Masterworks take care of storage, insurance, and eventual sale. When the artwork is sold, investors share the profits based on their ownership.

Yieldstreet stands at the intersection of innovation and alternative investments. It offers a smorgasbord of unique investment opportunities, ranging from art to marine finance. For those looking to venture beyond the beaten path of traditional stocks and bonds, Yieldstreet presents a tantalizing array of options.

The platform’s allure lies in its curated selection of alternative investments, each vetted by experts. This ensures that while investors are treading unconventional grounds, they’re not stepping into the unknown blindly.

Investors begin by browsing through the diverse investment opportunities on Yieldstreet. After selecting their preferred asset class, their funds are pooled with other investors and allocated to the chosen venture. Returns are generated based on the performance of these assets, be it through interest, dividends, or asset appreciation.

AcreTrader, as its name suggests, brings the vast expanses of farmland to the investment table. It offers a unique opportunity to invest in agricultural land, combining the stability of real estate with the evergreen nature of agriculture. With the global population on the rise, the value of fertile land is only set to increase.

The platform meticulously vets each piece of land, ensuring only the most promising plots are available for investment. This rigorous process ensures that investors are planting their funds in fertile ground, poised for growth.

Investors peruse available farmland listings on AcreTrader. After selecting a plot, they can invest, effectively owning a portion of that land. AcreTrader manages all aspects, from liaising with farmers to ensuring optimal land use. Investors earn from the appreciation of land value and potential rental income.

EquityMultiple is a testament to the power of collective investment in the real estate sector. By leveraging the principles of crowdfunding, it offers a platform where multiple investors can pool their resources to finance high-quality real estate projects. This collaborative approach allows for diversification and access to projects that might be out of reach for individual investors.

The platform’s strength lies in its curated selection of real estate opportunities, ranging from commercial spaces to residential properties. With a team of seasoned real estate professionals at the helm, EquityMultiple ensures that each project is vetted for maximum potential and minimal risk.

Upon joining, investors can explore a variety of real estate projects. After committing to a project, their funds are pooled with other investors to finance the venture. Returns are generated through rental incomes, property appreciation, or the successful completion of development projects.

CrowdStreet stands as a pillar in the commercial real estate investment domain. With its vast experience and industry connections, it offers a platform where investors can tap into prime real estate projects across the nation. From bustling urban centers to tranquil suburban locales, CrowdStreet provides a diverse range of investment opportunities.

The platform’s expertise ensures that each project is meticulously vetted, offering a blend of potential returns and stability. For investors looking to delve into commercial real estate without the hassles of property management, CrowdStreet is an ideal choice.

After registration, investors can browse a myriad of commercial real estate offerings. Upon investing in a project, CrowdStreet manages the investment, providing regular updates and ensuring optimal project execution. Investors earn returns based on the project’s performance, be it through rentals, sales, or project completions.

Mainvest offers a refreshing twist in the investment landscape, focusing on the heart and soul of the American economy: local businesses. From quaint cafes to innovative startups, Mainvest provides a platform where investors can support and benefit from the growth of small businesses in their communities.

The platform’s community-centric approach ensures that investments are not just about returns but also about fostering local economies. For those looking to make a difference while earning, Mainvest presents a unique opportunity.

Investors can explore various local businesses seeking capital on Mainvest. By investing, they essentially buy a revenue-sharing note, earning a percentage of the business’s gross revenue until a predetermined return is achieved.

Vinovest uncorks the world of wine investment, offering a blend of luxury, history, and financial growth. Fine wines have been a symbol of opulence for centuries, and Vinovest provides a platform where this luxury becomes an accessible investment.

With a team of wine experts guiding the way, the platform ensures that each wine is not just a drink but an investment poised for appreciation. From sourcing to storage, Vinovest handles every facet, ensuring the wine’s value grows over time.

After signing up, investors set their preferences and investment amounts. Vinovest then curates a wine portfolio based on these preferences, handling sourcing, authentication, and storage. As the wine appreciates, so does the investor’s portfolio.

Arrived Homes offers a fresh perspective on real estate investment, focusing on the charm of single-family homes. While skyscrapers and commercial complexes often dominate real estate discussions, single-family homes offer stability, consistent returns, and a touch of nostalgia.

The platform’s strength lies in its focus. By concentrating on single-family homes, it offers investors a chance to tap into a stable real estate segment, benefiting from both rental income and property appreciation.

Investors browse available properties on Arrived Homes. After selecting a property, they can invest in shares, representing a portion of the home’s value. As the property is rented out, investors earn a share of the rental income. Additionally, any appreciation in property value benefits the investors.

RealtyMogul stands tall in the commercial real estate investment landscape. It offers a platform where diversification meets opportunity, presenting a range of commercial properties for investment. From bustling office spaces to serene residential complexes, RealtyMogul provides a plethora of options for investors to expand their portfolios.

The platform’s prowess lies in its dual approach. Investors can either dive into non-traded REITs or make direct investments in specific properties. This flexibility ensures that both novice and experienced investors find opportunities that align with their investment goals.

Upon joining RealtyMogul, investors can choose between REITs or direct property investments. Their funds are then channeled into these real estate ventures. Returns are generated through rental incomes, property sales, or successful project completions.

The world of accredited investing is dynamic and ever-evolving. Emerging trends suggest a shift towards democratizing investment opportunities, with regulatory bodies considering more inclusive criteria for accredited investor status. This shift aims to balance the need for investor protection with the recognition that financial acumen can come from experience and education, not just wealth.

Furthermore, technological advancements are playing a pivotal role. The rise of blockchain and tokenized assets, for instance, is creating new avenues for investment and might reshape the landscape of opportunities available to accredited investors.

As the line between traditional and alternative investments blurs, the future promises a more integrated, inclusive, and innovative environment for accredited investors.

Understanding the role and opportunities of accredited investors is crucial in the modern financial landscape. While the distinction offers privileged access to unique investment opportunities, it also comes with increased risks and responsibilities.

As the world of investing continues to evolve, potential accredited investors are encouraged to stay informed, conduct thorough research, and seek professional advice. The realm of accredited investing, with its blend of challenges and opportunities, promises exciting prospects for those ready to navigate its complexities.

Ian Ippolito, a former professional software developer, is an investor and serial entrepreneur. He founded Private Investor Club and The Real Estate Crowdfunding Review, where his five-part series on AI and investing begins here.

For years, I dismissed AI as hype. Then in February 2026, it finished in a few hours the Monte Carlo program for our family’s finances that had defeated it for months. Since then many have been surprised at how expensive and scarce AI is turning out to be. Here’s what I found, and how it’s changing where I invest.

(Disclaimer: I’m an investor sharing my personal opinion. I’m not your attorney, accountant or financial advisor, so consult your own professionals before making any financial decisions.)

Before starting companies, I worked as a professional software developer. Later I founded and sold vWorker (formerly Rent a Coder), an early online marketplace for hiring programmers.

Today I run Private Investor Club, where accredited investors share due diligence on private investments.

So when AI companies claimed their tools could write software, I tested the claim myself. In the fall of 2025, I used AI to help build a Monte Carlo simulation for our family’s finances: the kind of program that runs thousands of what-if market scenarios, which many of you have used to test your own retirement plans.

It was miserable. The AI forgot what it had done a few minutes earlier, ignored instructions and broke code that already worked. After a few months of workarounds, I gave up.

By December 2025, I expected AI to join the long list of technologies that never lived up to their hype. And I thought an ugly stock market correction was coming.

In February 2026, an acquaintance mentioned that Anthropic’s Claude Code had improved a lot, so I gave it one more try, fully expecting to be disappointed.

I handed it the half-finished Monte Carlo program. It finished the job in a few hours, and the code was clean and worked.

Then I gave it something harder. In 2024, my wife and I went shopping for a lot to build a home on, and quiet matters a lot to us. So I paid a talented overseas developer $3,500 to build a program that tracks airplane flights over different parts of town. He did excellent work in six weeks.

I gave Claude Code the exact same requirements. It built the whole program in about five hours, for roughly 69 cents’ worth of my $100 monthly subscription. It even caught an error in a data provider’s documentation that I had missed, and it added useful features I hadn’t asked for.

I spent decades learning to program. Watching a machine do that work faster and better than a very good human developer was both thrilling and a little sad.

When AI redoes a $3,500 programming job for 69 cents, it looks like a nearly free substitute for human workers. Plenty of executives had been saying exactly that for years:

The predictions had a real basis. AI is priced by the “token,” a small piece of text the AI reads or writes, and the price of each token really has collapsed. In early 2025, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman estimated that the cost of a given level of AI drops roughly tenfold every year (Three Observations).

But the newest AI models chew through far more tokens to finish each task. So the price per token can keep falling while the total bill keeps climbing.

The research firm Gartner now expects AI programming to end up costing more than the staff it was supposed to replace. In June 2026 it forecast that by 2028, companies will spend more on AI coding than the average developer earns, because models are consuming more tokens and vendors are moving to pay-per-use pricing (Gartner).

Even if tokens keep getting cheaper, AI runs on land, buildings, permits and electricity. And all four are getting scarcer.

Local communities are fighting new data centers:

Electricity is the other bottleneck. The consulting firm ICF forecasts that U.S. electricity demand will grow about 25% between 2023 and 2030 (ICF). Data centers are competing for that power with electric cars, heat pumps and new factories.

My view is that AI will stay scarce and expensive for a long time. Cheaper chips can’t conjure up power plants, transmission lines or a permitted data center overnight.

So I’m looking at two kinds of investments: the things AI can’t run without (the first three below), and the work AI still can’t do (the fourth). Physician on FIRE has covered the public-market side in Investing In The AI Revolution; my focus here is private deals.

In each area, I’ll start with the deals that didn’t make it through my due diligence, and then the ones that did.

1. The AI companies themselves. Every one of those runaway AI bills is income for whoever sells the AI.

I passed on two fast-growing startups, one claiming its revenue was multiplying about fourfold a month, because I thought the big AI developers, such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, could add what they do as a feature. I also passed on a fund aimed at mid-stage companies, which are riskier (though the winners can pay more).

Where I did invest is a fund focused on later-stage AI and robotics companies (ones already selling at scale, with more history to judge), and by extension several AI companies:

2. The buildings and networks AI runs on. When billions of dollars of new data centers are blocked or delayed, the ones already approved, powered and operating become harder to replace.

The one that passed is a fund that owns income-producing data centers leased to tenants with strong finances, on long leases with built-in rent increases. I intend to invest.

3. The energy that feeds them. Data centers need reliable power, whether it comes from natural gas, renewables or nuclear.

In oil and gas, I liked a fund that buys mineral rights, which collect a share of what wells produce without paying to drill them, and can be lower risk than drilling. I went from AI skeptic to believer in 2026, and I expect AI to rank among the most economically important technologies of the coming years. And the prediction that it would be a cheap replacement for people hasn’t held up so far, as the companies that acted on it have learned from their bills.

#8585. Claim Your Carrier’s Autopay Discount – Pay From Checking, Not a Credit Card

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile take $5 to $10 a month off each line when autopay pays the bill from your bank account, and Verizon and AT&T also require paperless billing. No credit card qualifies except the carrier’s own. Put the bill on autopay from checking unless your card’s rewards and cell phone protection are worth more than the discount.

On a four-line family plan, $10 off each line comes to $480 a year.

Which payment method qualifies depends on the carrier. Verizon takes up to $10 off each line on its current unlimited plans when autopay draws from a bank account, and a debit card no longer qualifies. AT&T takes $10 off each line for a bank account and $5 for a debit card. T-Mobile takes $10 off each phone line on its current T-Mix plans for either one. Older plans can carry a smaller discount, so check the discount line on your bill.

Say a family on that plan pays its $160 monthly bill with a card earning 2% back. The card earns about $38 a year, so paying from checking instead leaves the family about $440 ahead.

The case for keeping the card is cell phone protection, which some cards provide only while you pay the phone bill with them. If your card covers your phones and you’d otherwise buy your carrier’s protection plan, keep paying by card when that plan costs more a month than the discount saves.

To switch, open the autopay settings in your carrier’s app or online account and add your checking account as the payment method, with its routing number at hand. Turn on paperless billing at the same time. The discount starts within a bill or two. After that, let autopay make every payment, since at Verizon and T-Mobile even a one-time payment by credit card can cost you the discount on the next bill.

AT&T and T-Mobile can take the payment from your bank account about two days before the due date. Keep at least one month’s phone bill in checking beyond what your other automatic payments need, and open each bill when it arrives so you can dispute a wrong charge before it’s paid.

If it feels like there are more millionaires in the U.S. than ever before, you’re right. However, most millionaires don’t have $1 million in their checking or brokerage accounts. The bulk of their wealth is tied up in their home equity and retirement accounts. If we excluded both, the number of millionaire households in the U.S. would drop by over 50%.

It takes time to build wealth. Young people have time. In general, they will use that time to earn income, save for the future, and benefit from compounding. That time is an opportunity, although people differ in their ability to use it. As we get older, we can accumulate more financial wealth. But we also have less time left. Most older people would gladly trade some of their wealth for more time.

Retirement is increasingly becoming a touchy topic for many, especially those of us who are used to a certain level of stability. A New York Life survey of more than 2,000 adults found that 34% had already delayed retirement or planned to, and 46% of them expected to push it back 5 years or more. Their top reasons were a lack of savings (46%) and inflation (45%).

Here are some common and dangerous assumptions that individuals make when planning for retirement: stock and bond market returns will be robust, inflation will be benign, you’ll be able to work past age 65, and you will receive an inheritance. Here are some ways to avoid them.

In the financial independence community, people often struggle to identify their true purpose. Many people assume globe-trotting should be their ultimate goal, yet they find it does not fulfill them as much as they expected. How do you know if travel is a genuine purpose or just a distraction? Ask yourself these three questions.

The bull case for housing is the fact that we simply aren’t building enough houses. There’s also a strong possibility we will experience a surge in housing activity if and when mortgage rates fall to a more reasonable level.

Health flexible spending accounts, or FSAs, are tax-advantaged accounts that let workers set aside pretax money to cover eligible health expenses. However, they’re often use it or lose it, with unspent balances forfeited at the end of the plan year.

Every January, a physician somewhere learns about a tax strategy that would have saved them $40,000. Would have. The deadline was December 31, and nobody mentioned it until the W-2 landed.

That’s the whole trap of earning a high salary with no business attached. The money shows up, the withholding leaves, and you assume the gap between gross and net is simply the cost of being a doctor. You max the 401(k). You do the backdoor Roth. You feel responsible. Then you write a six-figure check to the Treasury and wonder why the radiologist down the hall seems so relaxed.

#8583. Keep Rent & Utilities Near 30% of Gross Pay – Then Test Your Real Budget

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Start from 30% of your monthly pay before taxes for rent and utilities together. Past that, the federal government counts your housing as a burden. Then add renter’s insurance, parking, and your commute, and check that take-home pay still covers your debt payments and savings. If it doesn’t, aim lower before you sign a lease.

A landlord’s approval won’t tell you whether you can afford a place. Many landlords ask for monthly income of three times the rent, which allows rent up to a third of your pay and ignores utilities.

The federal government’s line is tighter than the landlord’s. The Department of Housing and Urban Development treats housing as a burden once it costs more than 30% of monthly income, utilities included. Rent at 30% of your pay crosses that line once you pay for power and water.

That 30% is also figured on gross pay, before taxes, so rent at that level takes more than 30% of the paycheck that reaches your account.

To test a place, add up everything it costs each month: rent, utilities, renter’s insurance, parking, and the commute from that address. Subtract that total, your debt payments, and your monthly savings from take-home pay to see what’s left for groceries, your phone, and everything else. Then save the security deposit and first month’s rent you’ll need to move in.

In high-cost cities, 30% of your pay may not rent much on your own. A roommate who splits the rent and utilities can put a pricier place within reach, and an address near work can justify higher rent if your commute costs fall by as much as the rent rises. A cheaper neighborhood works too, as long as it saves more on rent than it adds in travel.

Aim lower if you’re paying off student loans or card debt, or building savings. Say you earn $54,000 a year, pay $300 a month on student loans, and spend $150 a month getting to work. Thirty percent of your $4,500 monthly gross is $1,350 for rent and utilities, and with the loans and commute you’d spend $1,800, or 40% of gross pay. Holding rent and utilities near $1,100 instead of $1,350 cuts that total to $1,550 and leaves $250 a month, $3,000 a year, to save.

If what’s left of take-home pay can’t cover groceries and your other bills, the rent is too high, whatever the landlord approves.

Track your spending with one of the best budgeting apps so the test uses your real numbers.

A campsite in a state or national park costs a fraction of a hotel room, but popular campgrounds can fill the day reservations open. Book on Recreation.gov or your state’s park reservation site that morning, buy an annual pass if you’ll visit several parks, and borrow gear for your first trip.

A tent site at Bryce Canyon National Park costs $30 a night, while U.S. hotel rooms averaged $160 a night in 2025, according to CoStar. For a seven-night trip, that’s $210 for the campsite against $1,120 for the room.

The hard part is getting the site, since some popular campgrounds can book up within minutes. Recreation.gov takes reservations for campgrounds in national parks, national forests, and other federal lands. Most of its campsites go on sale six months before arrival, usually at 10 a.m. Eastern. State park campsites book through each state’s own reservation site, on its own schedule, such as 120 days ahead in Minnesota.

For a trip just weeks away, look for campgrounds that take reservations only a short time ahead, such as Bryce Canyon’s Sunset Campground, which books no more than 14 days before arrival.

The America the Beautiful pass costs U.S. residents $80 and covers one car’s entrance and day-use fees for a year at national parks, national forests, and other federal lands, though not campsite fees. Three parks charging Yellowstone’s $35 a car would cost $105 in entrance fees, more than the $80 pass, so buy it when you’ll visit three or more. Some states sell their own park pass, such as Minnesota’s $35 year-round vehicle permit, which costs the same as five $7 day permits.

For a first trip, borrow or rent the tent and sleeping bags, and buy your own once you know you’ll go again. Or skip the tent and rent a camper cabin, which Minnesota’s state parks offer for $80 to $90 a night, about half the $160 average hotel rate.

Look up the date and hour your campground’s sites go on sale, on its Recreation.gov page under Seasons and Fees or on your state’s reservation site, and log in well before then.

In 1980, a benefits consultant named Ted Benna figured out how to use Section 401(k), a little-known provision Congress added to the tax code in 1978, to build the first 401(k) plan. It quickly became a favorite among companies looking to offer employees more retirement benefits.

Today, it is still the cornerstone of retirement planning in America. Even physicians who often have a 403(b), 457(b), or defined benefit plan available too, usually max out their 401(k) first.

Recently, Benna has made headlines for calling out his invention, the 401(k), for disproportionately rewarding the wealthy. He may have a point. But I still think the 401(k) is the best retirement account most workers can get, and that it’s still worth it for doctors.

Also read: Beyond the 401(k): Why Physicians Are Turning to Defined Benefit Plans

In a recent Bloomberg interview, Benna argued that the modern 401(k) has grown too complicated and too costly, and that it benefits wealthier savers more than middle- and lower-income workers, the people who arguably need it most.

Affluent employees can afford to max out an account and reap the tax break on top. Benna believes low-income workers either lack access to a plan or can’t afford to contribute if they do.

Research seems to agree. Researchers at Vanguard, Yale and MIT found that about 44% of employer matching dollars go to the top 20% of earners at their companies.

And the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics has reported that while 70% of private-sector workers have access to a defined contribution (DC) plan such as a 401(k), only 49% participate. That means roughly 3 in 10 workers who could use a plan but don’t.

Source: BLS. Alt text: BLS chart showing 70% of private-sector workers have access to a defined contribution plan and 49% participate, March 2026
