Thank you for raising this point. The lack of concern about the impacts on businesses has been a real source of frustration for me.

My day job has given me a window into some industry sectors, including during Trump 1.0 and the trade war then. I always remember the small US steel manufacturer one of my colleagues spoke with at that time, when researching some of the impacts of steel tariffs.

The company was an important employer in its local area, producing steel canisters that it sold to a global slate of companies (so it was an exporter, and also sold domestically). Its main input was a particular type of steel pipe made in China (so it was also an importer). After Trump implemented steel tariffs, this small firm was suddenly paying an additional $250 million (back in 2018/2019; do your own inflation math as to what that would be today) at the US border before it could pick up a shipment.

It wasn’t going to be able to afford to stay open if it couldn’t get the administration to give it a tariff exemption (something Trump 1.0 was more willing to do, although the time involved to apply and, hopefully, get some sort of relief (many didn’t) meant companies were shelling out cash in the meantime). Why? Because not only did it not have a way to source the pipe in the US (steel is made to specification and you often can’t just readily swap things out), it couldn’t afford to do that because with a global client base, it needed to keep its pricing competitive (its customers could seek out non-US sources, unaffected by tariffs, for canisters instead).

We do actually have a manufacturing sector in the US. Most companies in that sector are small and midsized firms (fewer than 500 workers; often much smaller) and these may be important employers locally (although most employment in the industry overall is via the smaller number of very large firms); many are family firms. All sizes of manufacturer may import a raw material, a component or a finished good (including capital equipment for their facilities). When we tariff, we end up hurting our own manufacturing sector along the way. I lost track of the steel canister-maker’s fate, but I’ve never forgotten its difficulty, as just one illustration of tariff impacts that aren’t about the CPI.

But there’s also no real controversy (among people who study this stuff) in saying that tariffs tend to raise prices somewhere along the way, although it can take several months and may not be a straight $1 for $1 increase for end-consumers (although it often, eventually, is). I agree that it doesn’t create a prolonged rise in inflation (which is a rate of increase), but it does tend to eventually raise prices over a certain period and they then stay at that higher level. That’s actually part of how tariffs work, by putting a new floor under prices, reducing price competition.

And there are spillovers well beyond the firms initially impacted. For instance, US makers of tin plate, used in can-making, were hit by Trump 1.0’s steel tariffs, which jacked up their input costs (whether they continued with imports or switched to domestic sources — especially since domestic steel makers raised their own prices after tariffs were imposed on imports, an approach they’ve continued with in the latest trade war). This then made foreign-produced end-products such as canned food more attractive, because the pricing was better due to the lower production costs for non-US producers of tin plate. In other words, not only did US tin plate manufacturers suffer, but so did their US customers, as those companies’ customers looked elsewhere. (Trump’s much-broader trade war this time could offset some of this, by making imported canned goods more expensive, as well, depending on how things play out, which, in turn, would affect things like grocery store margins, etc.)

I also want to add that one of the biggest problems worrying the manufacturing industry for years, including pre-pandemic, has been the difficulty firms often face in filling the jobs they already have, and the difficulty they expect to face in filling jobs they expect to have due to a looming wave of retirements. This is due to several reasons: a skills gap (applicants not having the desired skill-sets); geographic miss-matches (jobs in one place, potential workers in another); problems with drug use in some communities (applicants are often expected to pass drug tests in order to operate machinery; the opioid epidemic has truly clobbered some communities in manufacturing areas); lack of interest among younger people in going into manufacturing or other production sectors (definitely something we need to work on; lack of exposure and training in K-12 is part of the trouble there, although the appeal of other types of work has also pulled potential workers elsewhere — maybe AI taking white collar jobs will sort that out?); and an increasing tightness in the overall US labor market due to demographics (ie, retirements on the aggregate, although jobs involving manual labor often see retirements at earlier ages, skewing the problem for those industries).

To finally conclude this overlong comment — which still barely scratches the surface; I didn’t even go into the tariff (and trade war) impacts on US shipping and logistics sectors tied to global trade, including imports — a major and rarely-discussed downside of tariffs is simply that it’s so difficult to readily see the ways they thread through an economy and create a drag on firms’ employment, wages/benefits, expansion plans, financing options, earnings and stock prices, and, yes, on consumer spending. The hits to businesses are often below the radar — especially since many companies don’t want to attract the anger of protectionists (unions; certain parts of the progressive wing; the Trump administration) by openly admitting how tariffs hurt their business. So people who aren’t trade geeks are understandably oblivious to real effects of these types of policies. As Cullen Roche over at Discipline Funds has repeatedly put it, with tariffs, you have less economic growth than you would have had — you just don’t know it.

The Biden administration and Dems in Congress (and sometimes even GOPers in Congress at that time, in some rare moments of bipartisanship) did several good things to directly support certain manufacturing and other production sectors (in my world I knew about policy for clean energy-related manufacturing; the defense industry; critical minerals; computer chips). Trump and the GOP have reduced or eliminated a chunk of that, unfortunately. But the recent tax bill did include some useful items for manufacturing. The GOP could do even more to directly support the sector, if manufacturing jobs are the real goal of all this, without the downsides of tariffs. (To be clear, this is not a political argument that I’m making; I didn’t like the tariffs imposed during the Biden admin, any more than Trump’s.)

However, the more fundamental problem here is that the reason that things like this (i.e., Trump unilaterally going tariff-nuclear, which is actually quite similar to what Biden did trying to illegally wipe out student loan debt, it’s just that Trump’s actions are at a different order of magnitude) is because Congress actively refuses to do their jobs. In the last several decades they have rather been rather determined to pass really loose/broad laws and specifically leave the “details” to the executive branch (either as some nebulous presidential power, or via some rule-making provision for an executive agency). This was bad but not terrible as long as we were electing presidents who were within a standard deviation of the ‘center’ of the political spectrum. However, Trump is a major outlier, and now it is readily apparent that Congress’ approach of letting the executive branch decide most things for itself isn’t actually a really good idea.

Even going back to the difference between Trump’s use of tariffs and Biden’s student debt cancellation efforts, it is clear that Biden’s policy, while objectively of very dubious legality, didn’t move the macroeconomic needle. Trump’s policies, on the other hand, even if they turn out to be completely legal (which I’m not sure they will), are rather painful object lesson on why Congress needs to actually do their jobs with a bit more effort.

A stray bit of additional perspective: A good friend of mine lost a large swath of her extended family when covid churned through northern Italy in the first year of the pandemic. Communities in their area suffered terrible losses that upended the social fabric overall, in addition to the grief suffered by specific families.

This also happened in many parts of the US, with certain kinds of communities hit particularly hard (groups that tend to live with extended family were especially vulnerable; non-hispanic white middle- and upper-class America is least-likely to live that way, so people from that type of background may not have seen much of this directly).

Given what NYC itself went through early in that first year, it also wouldn’t surprise me if NYT staffers genuinely felt horrified at what was happening. My friends and colleagues living in NYC certainly felt that way, based on what they were seeing and experiencing directly themselves.

So yes, it’s absolutely true that all forms of heart disease combined remained the number one cause of death in both 2020 and 2021, followed by all cancers combined. But I suspect that many people whose families and communities were gutted by covid would agree with the NYT that the toll from that new cause of death was terrible, and that it was something worth being concerned about, even if covid alone ended up being the third-leading cause of US deaths in both of those years, after which broad herd immunity finally set in.

Also, if anyone has an idea for how to fund newspaper journalism such that eyeballs aren’t the thing, I know several very good journalists who would *love* to hear what it is. (Pricier subscriptions can’t be the answer; not if you want to pay decent salaries and thus keep people around so that you have a good mix of entry-level people and experienced folks, and not if you want to include small and regional news outlets in your funding model — you could never charge enough for subscriptions for a local or even regional paper for that to cover all costs and still have a decent staff, both in terms of actual size and experience mix. This applies to both digital and hard-copy papers.)

If you do not think that the NYT serves a political agenda, the you are naïve.

And while I think that Pete’s nostalgic comment (“Decades ago in a brighter age of journalism, there may have been a time when headlines were designed primarily to inform us…”) is equally naïve, he recognizes that today news organizations are driven by getting eyeballs on their content. The thing is, it’s always been like this. Certainly, the intensity has varied with times and places, but yellow journalism (the type of sensationalism that characterizes nearly 100% of mass media coverage today) originated in the 1880s in NYC. Back then the NYT didn’t lower themselves to that level, but it’s pretty obvious that today they are down there and they deserve to be compared to the likes of FoxNews, MSNBC, and so forth.

I think a useful comparison that illustrates something important about the NYT is to look at its news articles and compare them with those in the Wall Street Journal (owned by News Corp, by the way, as is Fox News). Both the NYT and WSJ are dealing with a crazy-ass environment for “newspapers” vs back in the day. And both approach their news journalism in a similar way, even if the specific type of news story they do may differ.

At the same time, nothing could be more different than their respective opinion sections — both the editorials by their editorial boards and those by columnists and guests are 180-degrees opposite from each other much of the time.

In other words, in terms of political-ish stance, they are radically different. In terms of journalism? Pretty similar: fact-based, attempting to give a full picture, and corrections if someone messes something up. They entertain if they can, but it’s secondary to information provision.

I can’t say the same about Fox News (which I used to watch some years ago, but stopped when I realized I was never really going to get a full picture of anything since it wasn’t their style). They are really an entertainment-first entity, and they are facing fierce competition from Newsmax, which has made it less and less appealing for them to say anything they think their viewers might not want to hear. (That said, I’ve found the online version of their sister product, Fox Business, to be helpful at times. Just as I like CNBC’s “state of freight” pages for some aspects of tariff impacts on shipping and warehousing. Written! Not the videos/cable shows for either of these. There’s usually more information in written material, and the potential for more nuance. (Not always fulfilled, alas).)

I think that there is a case to be made that sales taxes, above all other taxes, are the most “just” taxes. The idea is that sales taxes are the form of taxes that give the individual tax payer the greatest degree of economic freedom. Don’t want to pay so much in taxes? Then just buy less stuff!

This sort of thing is very difficult with other forms of taxes, because there aren’t reasonable ways to reduce property taxes, and in some cases (i.e., gentrification) your taxes can increase by huge amounts even if you do nothing at all but sit at home. Income taxes, excise taxes, and tariffs live in a bit of a middle ground (they provide a bit more economic freedom, but are still more difficult than sales taxes to deal with in terms of accomplishing the “I want to pay less tax” objective).

I agree wholeheartedly. Income tax punishes you for working. Property tax is pretty crazy, because it’s based on appraised value, and you can actually be the one who created the value, i.e. you buy raw land and build a house on it completely with your own hands and your taxes go up 1000-fold. Nobody helped you, but you now owe a dramatically higher amount of tax. Extreme (and rare) example, but illustrates how bizarre this type of taxation is. And of course, if you are renting, and the property owner’s assessment goes up, this is going to be passed on with a rent increase unless there is a rent control law, which will lead to a dilapidated building in need of repair, or people leaving the area, and many other problems.

I disagree with the word “regressive.” It oversimplifies and is biased language. The thing is, the phenomenon you’re describing is simply an effect of a person being rich. The same percentage added to the sale of a good treats everyone equally – the difference is one person is rich. It’s not “hurting” the poorer person, it’s just that the rich person has a lot of money…because they’re rich. And when it comes to income taxes, “progressive” taxation is not more fair, it’s less fair. A percentage is already “progressive” because of math – 10% of $100,000 is $10,000 and 10% of $1 million is $100,000 – 10 times more tax revenue for 10 times the income. That’s completely fair. The idea of confiscating an escalating percentage is not more fair.

The math changes if you consider the marginal value of a dollar to someone who is rich vs someone who is poor. A thousand dollars more or less to someone making minimum wage is significant when measured in how much it will impact their lives. A thousand dollars more or less to a multi-millionaire with a high six figure income is barely noticeable. I agree that a simple percentage tax is more “fair” if what you’re measuring is dollars, but I think it’s less “fair” if what you’re measuring is impact on someone’s life. That said, lowering taxes helps everyone.

That’s the whole point of earning more: the marginal value changes and you can afford more. Taxes are the same as groceries, or your house bills, or anything else. Money is fungible. By raising the tax rate on higher levels of income, you’re just advocating for redistribution of wealth.

It’s true that money is fungible in terms of what it will buy, but it’s not fungible in terms of life impact. Take $5K from someone who is barely scraping by and they might lose the roof over their head. Take $50K from someone wealthy and they will (justifiably!) be annoyed but it won’t put them on the street. In this case the $5K is more life changing than the $50K. I’d say I’m advocating for a tax regime that provides “more even distribution of pain (via lived experience)” rather than anything else, while still keeping taxes low enough overall to minimize disincentives for earning and building wealth. As you note below a “zero tax for people earning below a certain amount” does this and seems reasonable to me.

Most of the value in a piece of land comes from its location relative to amenities, jobs, etc. A piece of raw land in the middle of nowhere is not very valuable in this sense. I agree that it is valuable for the environment. A land value tax encourages people to make full use of valuable land, and thereby encourages density, leaving more people in cities close to each other and more land wild and open.

I think you have a stronger argument against a land value tax if your goal is to support and maintain suburban sprawl.

There are endless uses of land in all locations. Location relative to amenities would only fit one specific profile. Raw land in the middle of nowhere can be used for all sorts of things, too long to list, but suffice to say it’s worth a lot more than where houses can be built.

A noble reminder to not always believe the headlines. It seems, at least in our area, economic headwinds are harder to ignore. “Demand for unpleasant, repetitive low-wage factory work will increase, which should help raise the whole lower-income wage pool.”

I think this is more important than you give it credit for. Unfortunately, it would only happen if the tariffs were high, and stuck around long term – like decades, that just a few years.

Outsourcing is one of the largest reasons it’s challenging to be ‘middle’ class in this country without a college degree. A question to ask is: WHY is it cheaper to make something in China and ship it over 7000 miles by sea (at 200 tons of fuel per day) and a couple thousand more by land than the produce in locally? Because they have a minimum wage of an little as $235 per month, less than 1/4 of our federal minimum, no independent unions, and for the most part more lax environmental standards. Talking about the effects of competition has to take this into account – the playing field isn’t level. If they weren’t paying people 75% let’s for equal work, the cost of products would be similar, and after adding in shipping costs the local products would win most of the time. Outsourcing undermines our labor (and environmental) standards. It benefits the companies, but the benefit to consumers in the form of low prices comes at the cost of stagnating wages – low and middle wages haven’t kept up with inflation for decades. And it’s not just GM. First, they still have to compete with Ford and Chevy (and Tesla, etc). So they continue to innovate. But there’s also all of their suppliers (currently largely outsourced). And then every other product. It adds up. When all the thousands of jobs for making all of everything are all outsourced, it leaves all the people who would be doing that work to compete over those jobs that can’t be outsourced. When there are more workers than jobs, companies can offer less and less in compensation – and there are still people left over with no job at all. Cheap stuff at Walmart is not a worth while consolation prize to being laid off. Yes, robots will eventually take many of the outsourcable jobs. They may as well at least be American robots, where Americans can be the ones to do the maintenance and repair of them.

Considering Trump’s negotiating history, I think it’s overwhelmingly likely that these tariffs are mostly a negotiating tactic, and that we’re going back to mostly low tariffs and free trade once other countries lower their tariffs and trade barriers.

Trump has a long track record of initially talking tough and threatening to go nuclear in negotiations, then settling for a small incremental win. For example, when he threatened to blow up NAFTA in his first term. Then he settled for a very small win (rebranding it USMCA and some small but meaningful trade concessions.) Another example: he threatened to go “fire and fury” on North Korea. But he in the end basically maintained the status quo with some very minor concessions. I also think we should be discussing the UPSIDE to US stocks and our portfolios if these negotiations are successful. I think your article left out one big point. Trump raised the tariffs because other countries were charging up way more in tariffs than we charged them. His point was to even out tariffs.. even though he goes to extremes to do it. We should be paying lower tariffs for products from other countries in the long run after “the show” is over.

No, major trading partners like the EU charge on average minimal tariffs to US exporters, contrary to Trump’s aims.

With all due respect, you, and unfortunately, many others, are missing the point.

We (and Trump) get that the cost will get passed onto the consumers. Or at least that’s the “first order effect” (to borrow your phrase.)

What you’re missing is that consumers get to decide between whether to purchase the item or not. If they are willing to eat the cost, and the item is something they absolutely can’t live without, they’ll buy it. Or they won’t buy it at all.

In the latter case, the sales numbers (and thus revenue) of the company selling the goods will drop. At which point that company has a choice to make: live with the drop in sales, and thus bottom line, eat part of the tariff or all of it, in order to increase volume.

Obviously, the company’s goal (let’s use Nike as an example), is to make as much money as possible. So if they naively pass 100% of the cost onto the consumer, their sales might drop so much that they’ll realize that wasn’t the best financial decision. This is an optimization problem: find the global maximum. The variables are: what % of tariffs to eat (vs pass on), whether to continue to offshore or onshore (and to what degree), and so on.

Using the Nike example (because they recently sobbed about their $1Bn tariff bill), their product is, among other things, athletic shoes. They’re not an essential item. They’re a luxury. It’s also not something you buy every week. Consumers can easily forego purchasing a new pair of Nike shoes, and Nike can decide if it can stomach the sales drop or not and react accordingly. That’s not our concern. We shouldn’t feel sorry for Nike who got rich at the expense of exploiting sweat job labor and pocketing the enormous margins, while selling out American jobs.

The other second-order effect you missed is the fact that by creating these “tariff walls” the money stays onshore. I.e. customers buy US-made goods and pay local companies, i.e. their fellow citizen. The money feeds back into the US economy. Without them, even though goods are “cheaper” for the consumer, the money flows out of the country: enriching China and other third world countries at our expense. What are some third-order effects you think might arise from that? I hope you see how this thinking is a bit short-sighted.

Of course, if one’s goals are not to support and protect the USA and its people, then the above will seem silly and pointless (or even absurd!). But of course I’m writing this with the (naive) assumption that a US citizen cares about the well-being of their country and fellow citizen (I know, crazy.)

Your analysis was overly simplistic which had you naively conclude that Trump is a raving idiot when perhaps you’re missing a substantial portion of what is really going on.

First off, I fully agree that it is a good thing for Nike to be hit by the tariffs a bit. No harm done as they are just producing overpriced stuff nobody needs. Good thing that is bought less, maybe the saving-up a few people do by skipping that brings them nearer to the concepts that MMM is describing in this blog.

Regarding the point of money staying onshore, I do not think I have fully understood it and humbly ask if you could more elaborate on it for reducing my level of ignorance?

Though not as bad as for these guys ( https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Japan ), the population of the US is aging ( https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_the_United_States ). An aging population will always mean that the ratio between the number of people who can contribute to providing the labor for producing all goods and services consumed by the society (I would at this point assume that there will not be a sudden shift and many people seeing what MMM is telling – that most of that is actually not required and just keeps them poor and unhappy) and the number of people who consume these goods and services is getting worse. Meaning the amount of consumed products of labor remains constant but the amount of labour for producing these products decreases. Maybe an aging population will also require larger amounts of labour for providing things like elder care.

Now, shifting production of things like the mentioned shoes (though maybe ones that have a better cost-to-value ratio than the insane Nike ones), clothing and similar things elsewhere will obviously reduce the amount of labour that needs to be spent on producing these. So considering that demand for labour is (or as obvious by demographics soon will be) larger than the amount of labour available, it sounds like a good thing to me that customers buy non-US goods? These goods did not need to be produced with precious US labour so that labour can be put to better uses?

Also, I did not quite understand the point of money flowing out being a process that enriches other countries. I mean, money in the end is just a piece of paper (or some bits stored on a computer hard drive). What is important is (as Adam Smith phrased it) the amount of labour that can be bought with it. Why should anyone accept money as payment for stuff if they could not buy other things with it in exchange? A trade deficit means that the other countries are receiving more money than they are paying. But what do they then do with it? First, “they” here means the central banks of the other countries as the companies that receive the dollars for the stuff they sell to the US will trade it to the central bank for their local currency. So the central banks of the other countries are amassing an immense amount of dollars which they are not spending on buying US products due to the trade deficit. And judging from data from these central banks, they seem to be doing mainly one thing with these. Buying US treasury bonds. Which I find interesting, because these bonds will return more dollars which they then spend on buying more bonds because the US is not producing enough interesting-to-them goods or services to trade these dollars for.

Sounds like actually a good system from US perspective to me? Buy stuff from the other countries for dollars and they will give these dollars back in the form of US treasury bonds that can be used by the US government to then again spend within the US, for building infrastructure or paying social security.

And we all know how the US treasury bonds will be paid back when they come due. By selling more US treasury bonds. Which seem to be in good demand as the central banks of all the other countries want to put their dollars to use in some way.

I think I once heard a saying: If you owe 2 million dollars to the bank, the bank owns you. If you owe 2 trillion dollars, you own the bank.

Replace “you” by “US” and “bank” by “other countries” in that and the whole situation looks actually quite good from an US perspective to me. So looking back, should one really be surprised of what Nixon did in 1971 ( https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nixon_shock )? I mean, why would the others buy treasury bonds that only give them back more dollars when they could trade the dollars they buy the bonds with for gold?

Can you please elaborate on in what way you see other countries being enriched by this system?

Well for one other nations will retaliate with their own tariffs, which will hurt US exporters and result in a likely slow down in global trade. Secondly the US can’t easily produce many goods and is reliant on imports (like Bananas) Thirdly, as MMM points out a reduction in foreign competition will result in less innovation and more price gouging amongst domestic producers.

It’s important to highlight that whilst all tariffs are sales taxes, not all sales taxes are tariffs. VAT for example, is most definitely not a tariff (or even non-tariff trade barrier) as it’s applied equally to imported and domestically produced goods and services. The average tariffs the European Union charged on U.S. exports were less than 2 percent, so there’s nothing reciprocal about Trump’s tariffs.

Tariffs were the original taxation vehicle for the Federal government, because they are a tax on consumption (vs production) and because they are quickly self-limiting; consumption of imported goods is far more elastic than earning an income and so government revenue from them falls quickly as tariffs rise “too high”. States are limited by competition. The 16th amendment uncapped the size of federal government and now here we stand. Many would gladly take tariffs in exchange for an income tax, but sadly we have both. Also, don’t forget the effect of AI on the market. I believe it’s massive.

Great post. But one small correction, tariffs are not only payed by the end consumers. Like every tax, they are partly paid by the supplier and the consumer, this means that everyone along the value chain will bear a share of the tariffs. How much each side pays depends on their respective elasticities. The more inelastic, the higher the share payed.

Before you take your phone abroad, check whether your plan already includes data where you’re going. If it doesn’t, download a travel eSIM from an app, since a week of its data can cost less than two days of Verizon’s or AT&T’s $12 day pass. Turn off data roaming on your U.S. line before you land.

With roaming on and no plan in place, Verizon charges its pay-as-you-go rate of $2.05 a megabyte, more than $2,000 a gigabyte. A $12 day pass from Verizon or AT&T still costs $120 for one phone over 10 days.

Verizon’s Unlimited Ultimate already includes data abroad, and T-Mobile’s Experience More includes 5GB of high-speed data in 215-plus countries and destinations, with 15GB on Experience Beyond. Frequent travelers get data in more than 200 destinations on Google Fi’s Unlimited Premium.

If yours doesn’t, buy a travel eSIM, which leaves your own number on the phone, from an app such as Airalo or Saily. For a couple’s 10 days in Italy, two Airalo eSIMs with unlimited data cost $64, against $240 for Verizon’s TravelPass on both phones, which also covers calls and texts. Calls and messages on WhatsApp or FaceTime use the eSIM’s data at no extra cost. For lighter use, Saily sells 10GB for Italy at $20.99, good for 30 days.

Before you buy, make sure your phone supports eSIM and isn’t locked to your carrier. On an iPhone, the About screen in General settings shows No SIM restrictions beside Carrier Lock when it’s unlocked, and only your carrier can unlock a locked one. Install the eSIM over Wi-Fi at home, then switch it on when you land, with data roaming on for that line only.

A local SIM card bought on arrival works too, but not in an iPhone 14 or later bought in the U.S., which takes only an eSIM. A day pass still makes sense for a trip of a day or two, since it keeps your own number working with nothing to install.

Turning off data roaming on your U.S. line keeps background apps from setting off a $12 day pass, but calls and texts still can. On AT&T, making or answering one call or sending one text abroad adds the pass automatically, as Verizon does on its Unlimited Plus and Unlimited Welcome plans. Call and text through WhatsApp or FaceTime instead.

Your phone bill runs above your plan’s advertised price because taxes, the carrier’s own fees, device payments, and add-ons are billed on top of it. Taxes and the carrier’s fees stay with the plan, so read your latest bill line by line and cancel the lines and add-ons you no longer need.

Verizon’s plan terms say taxes, other government charges, and the company’s own surcharges can add 16% to 58% to standard monthly charges. Only part of that is set by the government.

Taxes and government fees, such as the 911 fees some states and localities require, come with any plan. The carrier’s own fees only sound like taxes. AT&T’s Administrative & Regulatory Cost Recovery Fee is $4.99 a month per line, and T-Mobile’s Regulatory Programs & Telco Recovery Fee is $5.49 a month per phone line, or $21.96 across four lines. Verizon’s Administrative and Telco Recovery Charge rose from $3.78 to $4.69 a month per phone line on Nov. 15, 2026.

Some plans include taxes and fees in the advertised price instead. US Mobile, for one, lists its unlimited plans with taxes and fees included.

Go through the rest of the bill line by line:

Say a household pays $10 a month for an unused watch line, $13 for insurance on a paid-off phone, and $5 for an international add-on. Canceling all three saves $28 a month, plus the per-line fee and taxes on the watch line.

Then compare what you pay per line with the best cheap cell phone plans.

#8540. 8 Financial Independence Books – Start With the Math & Mindset, Then Pick Your Path

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Before you plan an early exit from work, read two or three of the books behind the financial independence movement, one for the investing math, one for how you think about money, and one on the path you’d take. Borrow them from the library first, and favor authors who invest in low-cost funds over ones selling a shortcut.

A forum thread on FIRE, short for financial independence, retire early, gives you one stranger’s spreadsheet. A book gives you a whole plan and the reasoning behind it, so you can see where it fits your life and where it doesn’t.

You don’t need all eight. A book on the math shows how much saving and investing it takes to leave work early, one on the mindset helps you keep at it for years, and one on a single path shows what those years look like. One of each gives you a plan to test instead of a pile of tips.

Judge any FIRE book you find later by how its author invests. A plan built on low-cost index funds, which own every stock in a market index, has nothing extra to sell you. One that only works with the author’s course, coaching, or trading system is selling a shortcut.

The eight below start with the math and the mindset, move on to five different paths, and end with a counterpoint on spending.

For more on investing itself, a few investing books for beginners go deeper on index funds, investor behavior, and stock picking.

Before you buy any of them, check what your library card covers, since thousands of libraries lend e-books and audiobooks free through apps such as Libby and hoopla. Then test whichever plan wins you over against your own numbers, starting with your savings rate, before you change anything at work.

#8539. Kitchen or Bath Remodel – The Cheapest Layout Is the One You Already Have

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Moving a sink, toilet, or shower is one of the priciest changes in a kitchen or bath remodel, since new drain, vent, and supply lines mean opening floors and walls, paying a licensed plumber, and pulling permits. Leave each fixture on the drain it uses now, and spend your budget on what you see instead.

Fixtures cost the same wherever they sit, so the money a new layout adds goes into pipes you’ll never see.

Drains run on gravity. The International Residential Code, the model code for houses, requires a sink’s or shower’s drain to drop at least a quarter inch for every foot it runs. Over 12 feet, that’s at least 3 inches of drop the floor has to make room for. Each fixture also needs a vent pipe nearby, so a long move can mean running a new one up through a wall.

The toilet is the hardest to move, since its drain must be at least 3 inches wide. Under a wood floor, rerouting that pipe can mean cutting and reinforcing joists. On a concrete slab, the floor has to be cut open and patched for any move.

So change what you see and leave the pipes where they are. A new toilet fits the old drain when it matches the rough-in, the distance from the wall to the drain’s center. A vanity, counters, tile, lighting, and paint all go in around the pipes you have. The same code’s list of work exempt from permits includes painting, tile, cabinets, and countertops. A relocated drain or supply pipe needs a permit and an inspection before the walls close.

Say a bid for a slab-floor bathroom adds $9,500 to put the toilet and a new shower on the far wall. Leaving the toilet alone and setting the shower in the tub’s spot, on a base made to drain where the tub did, keeps that $9,500 for the parts you see.

Move a fixture only when the layout fails you every day, like a kitchen sink with no counter beside it. Even then, keep the move to a few feet, toward the existing drain and vent.

Before you sign, have every bidder price the job twice, with each fixture where it is and with your new layout, so you see what the move alone costs.

#8537. Ground Ambulance Bill – The No Surprises Act Won’t Cap It, but Your State Might

The No Surprises Act protects you from surprise air ambulance bills but not ground ambulance bills. Before you pay a ground ambulance bill, check whether your state caps it, make sure your insurer processed the ride as an emergency, and ask the ambulance service for a discount or payment plan.

With private insurance, the No Surprises Act keeps an air ambulance from charging you more than an in-network one would, as long as your plan covers emergency care. What you owe a ground ambulance depends on your state’s law, which may cap the bill at what an in-network ambulance would charge you.

People in 22 states had some protection from surprise ground ambulance bills as of February 2026, the Commonwealth Fund found. But states can’t regulate self-funded employer plans, where the employer pays claims from its own funds, and 71% of workers with job-based coverage are in such a plan, according to KFF’s 2026 Employer Health Benefits Survey.

Say your state limits you to what an in-network ride would cost and your plan’s in-network ambulance copay is $150. A $1,800 bill for the part your insurer didn’t pay then drops to $150.

Ask your state insurance department whether a state law covers your ride and your plan. Your HR office, or the number on your insurance card, can tell you whether the plan is self-funded.

Next, check the bill against your explanation of benefits, the statement your insurer sends showing what it paid and what you owe. If the insurer denied the claim or processed the ride as a nonemergency, ask it to process the claim again as an emergency, and appeal in writing if it won’t.

Then call the ambulance service’s billing office to negotiate the bill. Many ambulance services are part of a fire department or a government agency. A federal advisory committee reported in 2024 that some public services, including those in Baltimore and Baton Rouge, waive patients’ share of the bill for emergency rides.

Ask whether the service cuts charges for residents or for financial hardship, and for a payment plan on whatever is left. Every step here can wait until after the ride, so never let worry about a bill delay a 911 call.

File your late tax return now. If you’re owed a refund, there’s no penalty, but file within three years of the deadline or lose it. If you owe, the penalty is 5% of the unpaid tax a month, up to 25%, though the IRS waives it automatically if you filed and paid on time the three prior years.

Say you don’t qualify for that waiver, pay nothing until you file, and owe $4,000. File five months late, and the penalties reach $1,000, a quarter of the bill, before interest.

Of that, $900 is the late-filing penalty. Paying late costs 0.5% of the unpaid tax a month, and when both apply, the IRS trims the filing penalty by that amount, so together they come to 5% a month. File within a month of the deadline instead, and the penalties come to $200, plus $20 for each month the tax then stays unpaid.

Once you’re more than 60 days late, the filing penalty is at least $525 or the full tax due, whichever is less, so on a small balance the penalty can match the tax itself.

The waiver is the IRS’s Automatic Exemption from Penalty. On a 2025 or later return, the IRS doesn’t charge either penalty as long as you filed and paid on time for the three prior years. It applies when the IRS processes the return, and a letter confirms it, so there’s nothing to request. Without that record, you can still ask the IRS to remove a penalty for reasonable cause, such as a fire, a serious illness, or a death in the family. Neither one removes the interest, which runs on unpaid tax from the April deadline and builds daily until you pay.

So file now, even if you can’t pay it all. Filing stops the 5% penalty from growing, and interest stops on every dollar you pay.

Pay what you can through IRS Direct Pay, which draws the payment from your bank account for free, and set up an IRS payment plan for the rest.

State law caps what you can charge as a notary for each notarization, at $10 or less in most states, so notarizing alone pays little. To earn more, charge travel fees for mobile appointments and qualify as a loan signing agent, since a loan signing typically pays $50 to $200.

A routine notarization takes 5 to 10 minutes, and its fee can’t exceed $2 per signer under New York law or $10 per act under Florida law.

No state caps a signing agent’s fee, because the job is more than a notarization. Lenders, title companies, and signing services hire you as a contractor to print the loan documents, meet the borrowers, notarize their signatures, and send the package back. The National Notary Association says the signing itself takes 45 minutes to a few hours, not counting travel.

At a signing, send every question about the loan’s terms to the loan officer, since a notary who isn’t a lawyer can’t give legal advice.

Fees for notarizing are taxable income, but the IRS’s Schedule SE instructions leave them out of self-employment tax, the Social Security and Medicare tax on work you do for yourself. That exemption covers the notarizations alone, so travel fees and the rest of a signing fee count as self-employment income. Record each signing’s notarization fees apart from the rest of its pay, and set aside part of every payment for tax.

Before a trip abroad, get a debit card that charges no foreign transaction or ATM fees. When you arrive, use it to take out local cash at a bank’s ATM, and pick the local currency over dollars when the screen asks. That withdrawal costs less than changing money at a counter or taking a credit card cash advance.

A card with no foreign transaction fee can pay for much of a trip abroad, but local transit, tips, and small purchases still call for cash in many countries. Where you get that cash decides what it costs you.

An exchange counter, whether at the airport, at your hotel, or at your own bank before you leave, sells currency for more than it pays to buy it back. Wells Fargo, for instance, says that gap includes a markup. The FDIC says paying by card is likely to get you a better exchange rate than converting cash. As for traveler’s checks, American Express no longer issues them.

So get cash with your debit card at a bank’s ATM, and check what your bank charges for that. Chase, for example, charges Total Checking customers $5 per withdrawal at another bank’s ATM outside the U.S., plus a 3% foreign transaction fee, so a withdrawal worth $500 costs $20 in fees. The machine’s owner can add a fee of its own. A debit card that charges neither fee saves that $20. Schwab Bank Investor Checking, for one, charges no foreign transaction fee and refunds ATM fees worldwide.

After that, take out a few days’ worth of cash at a time, since each withdrawal can carry a flat fee.

College students have a lot on their plate already, including the need to study to get good grades, participating in any number of on-campus activities and potentially working part-time to have some spending money.

That said, college students should also focus on their financial future, including steps they can take to build credit before they enter the workforce.

After all, having a credit history and a good credit score can mean being able to rent an apartment, finance a car or take out a loan, whereas having no credit at all can mean sitting on the sidelines until the situation changes.

Fortunately, there are all kinds of ways for young adults to build credit while they’re still in school. Some strategies require a little work on their part, but many are hands-off tasks that you only have to do once.

Make sure your student knows the basic cornerstones of credit building, including the factors that are used to determine credit scores. While factors like new credit, length of credit history and credit mix will play a role in their credit later on, the two most important issues for credit newcomers to focus on include payment history and credit utilization.

Payment history makes up 35% of FICO scores and credit utilization ratio makes up 30% of scores.

Generally speaking, college students and everyone else can score well in these categories by making all bill payments on time and keeping debt levels low. How low?

Most experts recommend keeping credit utilization below 30% at a maximum and below 10% for the best possible results. This means trying to owe less than $300 for every $1,000 in available credit limits at a maximum, but preferably less than $100 for every $1,000 in credit limits.

One step you can personally take to help a child build credit is adding them to your credit card account as an authorized user. This means they will get a credit card in their name and access to your spending limit, but you are legally responsible for any charges they make. Obviously, this move works best when you have excellent credit and a strong history of on-time payments and you plan to continue using credit responsibly .

While this step can be risky if you’re worried your college student will use their card to overspend, you don’t actually have to give them their physical authorized user credit card.

In fact, they can get credit for your on-time payments whether they have access to a card or not. If you do decide to give them their credit card, you can do so with the agreement they can only use it for emergency expenses.

Your child can build credit faster if they apply for a credit card and get approved for one on their own, yet this can be difficult for students who have no credit history. That said, secured credit cards require a refundable cash deposit as collateral are very easy to get approved for.

Some secured credit cards like the Ambition Card by College Ave even offer cash back1 on every purchase and don’t charge interest2. If your child opts to start building credit with a secured credit card, make sure they understand the best ways to build credit quickly — keeping credit utilization low and paying bills early or on time each month.

While secured credit cards are a good option for students with little to no credit get started on their journey to good credit, there are also credit cards specifically designed for college students. Student credit cards are unsecured cards, meaning they don’t require an upfront cash deposit as collateral, but charge interest on any purchases not paid in full each month.

Many student credit cards offer rewards for spending with no annual fee required as well, although these cards do tend to come with a high APR. The key to getting the most out of a student credit card is having your dependent use it only for purchases they can afford and paying off the balance in its entirety each billing cycle. After all, sky high interest rates don’t really matter when you never carry a balance from one month to the next.

“One of the safest ways for college student to build their credit by learning valuable money skills.”

While secured cards and student credit cards help young adults build credit with each bill payment they make, other payments they’re making can also help.

In fact, using an app like Experian Boost can help them get credit for utility bills they’re paying, subscriptions they pay for and even rent payments they’re making. This app is also free to use, and you only have to set up most bill payments in the app once to have them reported to the credit bureaus.

There are also rent-specific apps and tools students can use to get credit for rent payments, although they come with fees. Examples include websites like Rental Kharma and RentReporters.

The Fair Isaac Corporation (FICO) also notes that students can start building credit with their student loans during school, even if they’re not officially required to make payments until six months after graduation with federal student loans.

Their advice is to make interest-only payments on federal student loans along with payments on any private student loans they have during college in order to start having those payments reported to the credit bureaus as soon as possible.

“Making interest-only payments as a student will not only positively affect your credit history but will also keep the interest from capitalizing and adding to your student loan balance,” the agency writes.

Of course, interest capitalization on loans would only be an issue with private student loans and  Federal Direct Unsubsidized Loans since the U.S. Department of Education pays the interest on Direct Subsidized Loans while you’re in school at least half-time, for six months after you graduate and during periods of deferment.

College students don’t have to wait until they’re done with school to start building credit for the future, and it makes sense to start building positive credit habits early on regardless. Tools like a credit card can help students on their way, whether they opt for a secured credit card or a student card. Other steps like using credit-building apps can also help, and with little effort on the student’s part or on yours.

Either way, the best time to start building credit was a few years ago, and the second best time is now. You can give your student a leg up on the future by helping them build credit so it’s there when they need it.

Lifeline takes up to $9.25 a month off one phone or home internet plan if your household’s income is low or anyone in it gets SNAP, Medicaid, SSI, federal housing assistance, or a veterans pension. Apply through the National Verifier, Lifeline’s application site, then pick a company whose plan costs little or nothing after the discount.

Only about 8 million of the nearly 38 million households that qualify have signed up, according to USAC, the nonprofit that runs Lifeline for the Federal Communications Commission (FCC).

You qualify if your household’s income is no more than 135% of the federal poverty guidelines, a limit that Lifeline’s income table shows in dollars by household size. You also qualify if anyone in your household gets SNAP, Medicaid, Supplemental Security Income (SSI), federal housing assistance such as a Section 8 voucher, or the Veterans Pension and Survivors Benefit. A February 2026 FCC proposal would limit Lifeline to U.S. citizens and certain legal immigrants and could require a full Social Security number, but it isn’t final.

Each household, meaning everyone at one address who shares income and expenses, gets one discount, so a parent on SSI who lives alone can get their own. On qualifying Tribal lands, the discount is up to $34.25 a month.

Apply online through the National Verifier, by mail with a paper application, or with help from a phone or internet company that takes Lifeline. Oregon and Texas residents apply through their state’s Lifeline program instead.

Then use the Companies Near Me tool to find the companies serving your ZIP code, and compare what each charges after the discount, since some Lifeline phone plans cost nothing. Choose a plan with data, because phone service alone gets only up to $5.25. A retiree on SSI who puts the $9.25 toward a $15 prepaid plan with talk, text, and data pays $5.75 a month before taxes.

On a free plan, use the service at least once every 30 days, or the company can cut it off after a 15-day warning. Lifeline rechecks your eligibility every year, and a recertification notice left unanswered for 60 days ends the discount. Other programs offer emergency help with rent, utilities, and food.

Before you apply, gather a benefit letter issued in the past 12 months, a screenshot of your benefits portal, or last year’s tax return, since Lifeline can ask for proof.

It all started last winter when I innocently posted a review for a heated vest I had bought on Amazon. I was happy with this fun new way to beat the winter and wanted to share it with others, so I gave it five stars. But soon after I clicked “Submit”, I got an email from Amazon which said something like,

“Congratulations! You’ve been selected to join Amazon Vine for writing helpful reviews!”

I was already aware of Amazon Vine since I had seen product reviews from other people in the program – typically called “Vine Voices.” The basic idea of this program is that you can order stuff from Amazon for free, as long as you agree to review at least 80% of the things you order.

“Hey, that’s cool”, I thought, “Who doesn’t like free stuff?

Especially since I’ve already been writing product reviews out of the goodness of my heart – why not be rewarded for it?”

So without giving it much further thought, I clicked “accept” on their terms and conditions and joined the program.

And so began a saga that has taken me on a surprising journey over the past nine months causing me to:

Okay, I’ll admit that there were also some upsides. My original idea was partly to save some money, by getting stuff I genuinely would have bought anyway, in a way that sounded fun. And that did happen – I saved at least a few thousand dollars on tools and materials for my construction business and the MMM-HQ Coworking space, for free. Plus, at least some of the motivation for signing up was to put myself through an experiment so I could write this blog article about it. And if you’re reading this, it looks like that happened too.

But I was still surprised at how powerful the combination of small nudges and incentives from Amazon was able to hijack my frugality instincts –  and get me to do a bunch of work that wasn’t really the best use of my time.

So I figured if we review my journey and break it down with a bit of Behavioral Science, we could all learn a few valuable things by laughing at Mr. Money Mustache’s folly.

Scarcity Brain and the Online Casino Effect

One of the most interesting books I’ve read in recent years is Michael Easter’s Scarcity Brain. It’s an exploration of the sneaky ways that modern gambling platforms, marketing and social media algorithms are all built upon two weaknesses in our evolutionary programming:

As I look back now, I realize that I fell straight into those same traps, because the Vine program has all the key properties of a casino or a TikTok feed:

Every time you log into the exclusive “reviewers only” Vine website, you’ll see different stuff available for the taking. Sometimes there is almost nothing worthwhile – you’ll search for “porcelain plates” and get endless pages of pink plastic disposable party plates instead. You look for a toaster for your kitchen but instead there will be just a toaster cover with a cat wearing a witch hat. WTF!?

But occasionally, there will be genuinely useful things like super nice light fixtures, tools and plumbing parts, an EV charger, and even some clothing. My favorite ridiculous Eagle shirt as featured in the Mustachianism music video was an Amazon Vine find.

As were a whole supply of super-realistic artificial plants, which while tacky in principle, have been amazing for hard-to-water courtyard garden areas at the MMM HQ.

I also had a lot of fun roping in friends and coworkers from HQ to help and share in the bounty. I let them help me request and review stuff that they wanted, and then they got to keep it. This seemed like a win/win because we shared the work and the fun of laughing at some of the ridiculous products available.

Still, as I went through this experiment this spring and summer and allowed the system to coax me into doing 80 reviews so I could upgrade my account from Vine Silver to Vine Gold*, I noticed something didn’t feel quite right.

I was checking the Vine page every day for scores, even when I didn’t actually need anything. It would usually be a bust, but just often enough, something I actually wanted would come up, and I’d order it before it was too late. Scarcity and unpredictable rewards at work.

Then the bounty would come, I’d unpack it and photograph it with assembly-line speed so I could batch-write all the reviews once per week or so. For every review I did, I was spending time I’d rather spend doing something else. And for every questionable item I got, I was creating pollution and trash from its manufacturing and packaging – directly contradicting the main values of my life and my reason for writing this blog. And I saw all of this, yet I kept doing it!

During the worst of this consumerism bender, things were dire. I was getting packages almost every day and my recycling bin was overflowing with cardboard. My son and my girlfriend started laughing at some of my more frivolous purchases, so I found myself discreetly tucking away the boxes when they were around to evade scrutiny.

But eventually, I moved into a recovery stage. I had been letting this habit continue out of laziness and as a form of procrastination: it’s very easy to order shit online and pretend I’m doing something useful, and much more difficult to get moving to do the things that really make my life enjoyable.

But I’m old enough to know that hitting the running trails and the gym for my daily workouts, and making progress on all my construction projects, and focusing on the computer as a creative tool rather than an entertainment device so I can get stuff done like this blog post, are the things that bring me the most joy.

Admittedly, some of the sucky factors of the Vine program helped make it easier to recover too. For every genuinely useful thing I found like a contractor-grade extension cord, I had to scan through endless screens of trinkets which not only wasted my time but actually pissed me off at their very existence.

I also noticed some of the deliberately reviewer-unfriendly features built into the program which reminded me that we reviewers are definitely just low-wage workers rather than any form of VIP. The search functionality is crap, and there is no way to filter or sort the results, because they want you to have to look through everything and they don’t care about the value of your time.

Then there is the hilariously bureaucratic AI-based evaluation system which would occasionally flag my totally tame, factual reviews as “Not meeting our Community Standards” without explaining what the problem was. So I’d have to go in and edit my review, randomly changing a couple of words and maybe some punctuation, and suddenly the AI would be pacified and accept my review. Just dumb.

It dawned on me that for many people, this is just what “work” looks like. You are given a bunch of tasks and a bunch of rules to follow, in a system you didn’t create and don’t get much say in changing. And then as long as you crank out your TPS Reports without rocking the boat too much, you get your paycheck.

It reminded me of the Uber Driving experiment I did way back in 2017: as soon as I started working as a driver, I could immediately see dozens of improvements that could be made to the system that would make it function better for both drivers and passengers. But since I wasn’t the boss, nobody wanted to hear my ideas.

Experiences like these remind me that while I love hard work and I love learning new things every day, I greatly prefer being the boss. And I’ve gotten pretty damned accustomed to it after 20 years of financial independence, so I see no need to give it up.

One interesting “gotcha” of the Vine program is that they do keep track of all the free stuff you get and send you a 1099 for its retail value at the end of the year. So it’s not really free, just discounted to whatever your marginal tax rate is (about 25% for me this year). If we peek into my account right now, this is how my 2025 is looking:

So I got about $7000 worth of stuff, and could owe up to $1750 of tax on it. In my case, about 75% of it was “sold” to my business for commercial use (construction supplies which I used on jobs or HQ renovations) so it was effectively converted into real income rather than just tax burden. Some of it was stuff I would have bought anyway for my own house which I’ll gladly pay the taxes on. But there is also probably about $1000 of pure nonsense in there as well, for which I’ll owe a tax bill of $250 as penance for my itchy trigger finger on that “Order” button.

Thanks to some advice from wise readers in the comments (below), I have since learned that in most cases you can mark down this estimated value by 80% before declaring it – because you have effectively eliminated most of the resale value by opening and reviewing the product. Thus my tax bill will be more like $50 rather than $250. More detail in this Reddit discussion here.

So here we are today. While I admit that I didn’t explicitly cancel my account, I used the “Keystone Habit” trick to override the temptation to view the Vine page – mapping that browser bookmark to my daily habits list instead, a little chart which I call my “Badassity Tracker”. The net result is that every time I click it, I’m taken straight to a reminder to get up from the computer and do a quick round of exercise, so I do that instead.

And of course my writing of this article may be a violation of the terms and conditions of the program (“the first rule of Vine is to not talk about Vine”), so it might even get canceled on me. (and if so I’ll let you know because that would be funny story as well)

But I learned a lot about habits and addiction, and realized that this same feeling might be what drives people into One More Year Syndrome, as they keep working even when they can afford to quit. I have now coached enough people through this situation to see it is way more common than I would have ever guessed.

As with all MMM articles, there’s a real life lesson in this story. It’s not really about Vine or me or my habits, it’s about you continuing to look at yourself and your life, and always questioning your own assumptions or patterns. And asking the people you trust most for feedback as well:

We will never be perfect, but the great news is we don’t have to be. All it takes is a little bit of self reflection and putting ourselves on a slightly better path, as often as we can as life goes on. We are all on a very long journey, so even a tiny course correction can make a huge difference in where we end up.

Facebook: if you use this URL when visiting, it will show you (mostly) just the stuff you want: https://www.facebook.com/?filter=friends&sk=h_chr

YouTube: If you use the Firefox browser and install the extension called “Unhook” it cleans up Youtube and removes all recommendations so you just watch the specific video you came there to watch.

Amazon is among many things known to be notoriously tax evasive (one small example is receiving 11bn in profits one year, paying 0% federal income tax on it). They unfortunately drastically undercount their carbon footprint and emit more carbon pollution than the approx 70 lowest emitting countries combined. Their annual CO2e emission is equivalent to emissions of about 18 coal plants in one year. They are the largest emitter of all the big five tech companies, contribute significantly to climate change and make billions from fossil fuel companies in addition to their data centers driving up fossil fuel demand.

Placing Amazon warehouses by the Interstate in order to repurpose valuable land for housing and bike trails would be the dream, though I am not sure it’s a realistic enough perspective to have on this company. Their warehouses are mainly located in communities of color (and their data center expansions are in oil and coal-dependent locations such as Saudi Arabia). These communities live up close to the environmental impact of Amazon’s emissions. It is easy to downplay or be unaware of the effects of something that is highly convenient for us, whether we consume a lot or a little (or an example of reasoning can be: yes, I am buying from a top polluter, but I only do it when I need something actually important to me). It shows most people on earth are not immune to this level of convenience. And consuming less is hard, but out of all companies, this one is a pretty big one in terms of pollution.

So to sum it up, it is great to consume less, though it doesn’t equate to Amazon being a clean company by far. For such an environmentally aware blog, that might be why it feels like this misses the mark, as Bumblebee pointed out.

The 50-20-0% rule for used products is something on the lines of:

50% FMV for name brand products 20% FMV for off brand/non branded name products 0% FMW for things you use for “business purposes for review, are broken or damaged, and are consumables that can’t be resold after opening

Using this rule, let’s say you bought $1000 worth of non branded stuff, you’d reduce FMV by $800. As the remaining resale value of the used products is now $200 using the 20% rule. You’d patties on $200, not $1000.

From all my research and extreme warnings from my CPA, this “50-20-0%” method is not a legally recognized tax strategy and carries massive audit risk.

The products we receive are legally considered non-employee compensation given to us in exchange for the service of writing reviews.

The IRS strictly requires taxpayers to report the Fair Market Value (FMV) of this compensation at the exact moment of receipt (though in practice, Amazon’s FMV is set at tine of ordering, not receipt).

Because you take immediate ownership of the item at its full value, opening and using it to write the review is legally considered personal use. Therefore, you cannot claim business depreciation or arbitrarily lower your 1099-NEC gross income for the “wear and tear” of opening your own compensation.

My CPA explicitly stated he will not file our taxes using fabricated internet depreciation formulas to arbitrarily lower a 1099-NEC.

Here is another discussion on the TurboTax forums where someone explains exactly why you cannot use this 50-20-0 rule and that there is no accepted way to manipulate the FMV of what you receive: https://ttlc.intuit.com/community/business-taxes/discussion/amazon-vine-1099-nec-schedule-c-deductions/00/3715093

The Vine program can easily cause a significant financial impact come tax season. Because Amazon issues a 1099-NEC, the IRS system automatically assumes this is business income subject to an additional 15.3% self-employment tax. When added to a normal ~25% income tax bracket, that creates a massive tax burden. For me, even living in Texas with no state income tax, I am still looking at roughly a 40% tax burden by default, which is brutal.

You can try to claim it as a hobby to avoid that 15.3% FICA tax, but overriding a 1099-NEC, moving it from schedule C to schedule 1, requires preparation to defend since the discrepancy because it can trigger an automated CP2000 notice.

For context, last year Amazon sent me a 1099-NEC with a massive $38,000 FMV for all my 2025 Vine items. (yes, the curse of making gold which means much more allowance and expensive >$100 items, such as a $1500 Gigabyte laptop amd $1k mini split AC, and a lot of other expensive gold exclusive items)

My CPA does not want to use the hobby declaration for that $38k because the sheer volume and daily review time makes it very hard to defend, even though I have not sold anything.

Beyond the tax classification, you must be extremely careful about Amazon’s published FMVs because they are often wildly inflated. Sometimes if you wait a few months, you will find that you could have purchased the exact same product outright for less cash than you are paying in tax liability through Vine.

This is why I am giving the warning that you have to do your homework before choosing things, sivh as checking price history and comparing to similar products. Buying outright means you only buy what you actually need, the item can be returned if you don’t like it, has a real warranty when it breaks, and you do not have to waste 30-60 mins writing a detailed review.

For example, I ordered a cold press juicer, even though I already own about nine other juicers, assuming the FMV was fair. I figured getting it for 40 cents on the dollar was a good enough deal. A few months later, the retail price dropped by about 75%. I ended up paying more in taxes for an un-warrantied, non-returnable item that I wasted an hour reviewing than if I had just bought it outright down the road.

In another instance, I selected a frozen drink slushie machine with an almost $300 FMV, meaning $120 in taxes for me. I spent a lot of time reviewing it, put it away, and then pulled it out months later to actually use it and found it was not freezing properly. I attempted to contact the seller but Amazon simply stated there is no warranty on a “free” product, making my $120 tax cost completely irrelevant. I also found that they replaced that product with a near identical model at a much lower, more competitive price.

I do not believe you can safely claim depreciation the way others have said, and even claiming hobby status to avoid the extra 15.3% FICA means going directly against Amazon’s 1099-NEC filing, requiring you to be ready to defend it. That said, I am now a much wiser Vine participant. I only select items that either have a $0 FMV or a very good one that is actually at or below actual value, and only if they are items that I actually need.

Actually, you don’t take “ownership” of the item until the 6-month mark, when you get the right of disposition, (if you cannot sell it nor give it away, you don’t own it). Before that the non-consumable item is the property of Amazon that you have been contracted to use & review in return for the compensation of the item in question at that 6-month mark. The item carries no value to you until then and when it does become yours, it’s value is depreciated from whatever FMV Amazon may set for a “new” item by virtue of its being used.

#8530. Budget a Renovation From Itemized Bids – Then Add 10% to 20% for Surprises

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Get two or three itemized bids on the same finished plan, then set your renovation budget at the bid you pick plus 10% to 20% for hidden problems like rot or old wiring. To stay under it, make every choice before demolition, get each change priced in writing, and pay from savings where you can.

Of the homeowners who renovated in 2025, 37% went over budget, the 2026 U.S. Houzz & Home Study found. More than half of them blamed products or services that cost more than they expected, and 35% had picked pricier materials than they first planned.

A budget built from a finished, priced plan makes both causes less likely. The bid prices what you’ll actually build, and the extra 10% to 20% is there for what nobody can see until the walls are open.

Say a couple’s chosen bid for a bathroom remodel is $18,000. They set the budget at $21,000, a $3,000 cushion, and when the crew finds rotted subfloor that adds $1,900, they finish $1,100 under budget without borrowing. Cash saved ahead in a high-yield savings account is the cheapest way to pay, since a personal loan or a loan against your home’s equity adds interest.

Then keep the plan from changing. Before demolition, choose every fixture and material, so you never pick in a hurry once the walls are open. Put each change in writing with its price before the crew starts it, and compare your spending with the plan every week.

Keep the cushion for hidden problems like that rotted subfloor, and pay for any upgrade you want midway by cutting a nice-to-have.

#8529. Adoption Grants & Interest-Free Loans – Apply After the Home Study, Before High-Interest Debt

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Apply for nonprofit adoption grants and interest-free loans once your home study, a social worker’s review of your household, is approved, and before you put fees on a credit card or take out a personal loan. Some grant funds won’t repay a fee you’ve already paid, and several stop accepting applications once your child moves in.

Helpusadopt.org, for one, applies each grant to an adoption’s final fees and won’t reimburse fees you’ve already paid, even with a card or loan. Charge the last $10,000 to a card, and a $10,000 grant has nothing left to cover.

Start with these five nonprofits, the first two open to families of any faith, marital status, or sexual orientation:

Helpusadopt.org, Show Hope, and Lifesong all need your application before your child moves in. Apply to several at once, since Helpusadopt.org still considers families who have won another grant.

Keep saving and fundraising while you wait, since Gift of Adoption looks for families who have saved and raised what they can. Raise money through a nonprofit’s page, such as Lifesong’s, rather than GoFundMe, so donors get a receipt. Then borrow only what’s left, on a monthly payment you’ve budgeted for.

Say a $5,000 grant and a $7,000 interest-free loan cover a $12,000 gap, and you repay the loan over four years. That’s $146 a month, $7,000 in all. Put all $12,000 on a card at 22% instead, near the average the Federal Reserve reports for cards that charge interest. Paying it off over the same four years takes $378 a month, about $18,150 in all.

Before your home study is approved, gather your latest tax return, two months of pay stubs, and a list of your assets and debts, and line up two references. Then your first applications can go out the week the approval arrives.

#8528. Out-of-Network ER Bill – You Owe Only Your In-Network Share

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

If your job-based or marketplace health plan covers emergency care, the No Surprises Act bars an ER and its doctors from billing you more than your in-network copay, coinsurance, and deductible, even when they’re out of network. Compare any ER bill with your insurer’s explanation of benefits, pay what it says you owe, and dispute the rest.

Say you have an emergency appendectomy at an in-network hospital, the surgeon is out of network, and your plan’s in-network coinsurance for the surgery comes to $250. If the surgeon then bills you $3,200, you still owe only the $250.

The No Surprises Act, in force since January 1, 2022, limits what you owe to that in-network share for care your plan covers in three situations:

The law leaves out ground ambulances, which can still charge out-of-network rates unless your state forbids it. You can give up the protection by signing a notice-and-consent form, a waiver that lets the provider bill you more than your in-network share. No provider may ask you to sign one for emergency care before you’re stable, and anesthesiologists, radiologists, pathologists, and assistant surgeons may never ask.

To spot a violation, compare the bill with your explanation of benefits, the statement your insurer sends after it processes a claim. The amount it says you owe should match the bill.

Call the provider’s billing office about any charge above that amount, cite the No Surprises Act, and ask it to cut the bill or refund what you overpaid. If it won’t, file a complaint with the No Surprises Help Desk online or at 1-800-985-3059, seven days a week, and the Help Desk can refer it to a state regulator.

While the complaint is open, pay the amount your explanation of benefits says you owe, and nothing above it.
